## Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Jimmy Buffett, Cultural Infidel" **·** John Dewey, Plato — Pragmatism; Experience and Education; The Meaning of Life — The editors argue Buffett is a philosopher despite his own denials, in the sense of Royce and Dewey: philosophy is critical reflection on living that returns to ordinary experience, and Buffett's songs, books, and concerts pass Dewey's test of rendering everyday predicaments 'more significant, more luminous, more fruitful.' They compare 'Margaritaville' to Plato's Republic — not equal in pedigree but equal in kind as occasions for philosophical practice — to defend meaning-making as a democratic practice open to Parrotheads, not just professors. Reading the album 'Changes in Latitudes, Changes in Attitudes' as a guide, they set Buffett's 'Porpoise Driven Life,' where purpose is found by sailing your own waters in the company of friends, against Rick Warren's revelation-based 'Purpose Driven Life.'
- ch. 6 "Coral Reefer Reason" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "That’s His Story and He’s Stickin’ to It" **·** Epicurus, Diogenes the Cynic — Epicurean Pleasure (ataraxia); Cynicism (living according to nature) — Aaron Pratt places Buffett's 'island escapism' in the lineage of the ancient 'graceful life' philosophies: like Diogenes the Cynic, Buffett flouts social convention (pirates over Civil War generals, the beach over the rat race, 'Be good and you will be lonesome'), and like Epicurus he preaches pleasure with prudence rather than mere indulgence. 'Cheeseburger in Paradise' becomes Epicurus's command to know what you want and go get it, while the hung-over confession of 'Margaritaville' — 'I know it's my own damn fault' — supplies the Epicurean proviso that overindulgence ruins the pleasure it promises. The chapter closes by arguing that counter-cultures like Parrotheadism carry built-in safety features: careers and families force Epicurean prudence, keeping escapism a periodic liberation rather than social collapse.
- ch. 8 "Too Much Tequila, Or Not Quite Enough" **·** Seneca, Ralph Waldo Emerson, Henry David Thoreau — Stoicism; The Dichotomy of Control — Doug Anderson reads Buffett as an 'American Stoic' — unlike his friend the Cynic Hunter S. Thompson, who dropped out and died, Buffett accepts his fated world of competitive capitalism and controls the one thing Stoics say we can: his own attitudes, 'changes in latitudes, changes in attitudes.' He leans on Seneca's advice to Serenus that wine and dreaming liberate the mind ('drink washes cares away') to interpret the dialectic of dreaming and drinking in 'Margaritaville,' 'Five o'Clock Somewhere,' and 'License to Chill' as Stoic self-renewal — the margarita even frees the singer to admit his own fault — with Emerson's intoxication-speaking poet as the American model. Excess is the failure mode: the expatriates of 'Banana Republics' who mistake the dream for an end state and Buffett's late-thirties hangover reckoning mark the Stoic middle path between deadening routine and 'too much tequila.'
- ch. 9 "Jimmy Buffett “Singer of Inordinate Tunes” and Heideggerian Troubadour" **·** Martin Heidegger, Emmanuel Levinas, Augustine of Hippo — Thrownness (Geworfenheit); Being-Toward-Death; Authenticity — Drew Dalton takes Buffett's claim that 'we don't just enjoy our escapism — we NEED it' as an admission that being itself is burdensome, overturning the Plato–Augustine–Leibniz consensus that it is good to be. Since 'Margaritaville is nowhere' — it is on no map and can never be reached — what we long for is not a better vacation but release from having to be at all, which is why even on holiday in Key West we still dream of escape. Heidegger's Being and Time supplies the framework: thrownness, being-toward-death, anxiety, and guilt reveal existence as a weight we never chose, so the escapist longing to be otherwise than ourselves is the 'inauthentic' flight Heidegger describes (without moral condemnation), and Levinas's On Escape confirms that 'it is precisely from all that is weighty in being that escaping sets forth.'
- ch. 10 "“Trip Around the Sun”" **·** William James, Henry David Thoreau, Bertrand Russell — Pragmatism; The Will to Believe — Phil Oliver pairs Buffett with William James: both hold that philosophy is 'not a technical matter' but each person's sense of what life deeply means, had in non-verbal moments of elevation as much as argued in words. The chapter's core is James's 'moral holiday' — a morally legitimate respite from care and struggle — naturalized in Buffett's 'License to Chill' and 'Trip Around the Sun' ('it's good to know it's out of my control'), joined by James's lightness about error from 'The Will to Believe' and Russell's and Dawkins's responses to cosmic annihilation. Against those who hear mere hedonism, Oliver insists Jamesian holidays are care-free but never care-less: like Thoreau's 'live deliberately' echoed in 'Growing Older But Not Up,' they renew us for the return to work, and James's ambivalence about alcohol in The Varieties of Religious Experience mirrors the risk of Buffett's frozen concoctions.
- ch. 11 "Parrotology" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "“Livin’ It Up”" *(no index entry yet)* — Amanda Feller reads Buffett's life and lyrics through Jack Mezirow's transformative learning theory: a disorienting dilemma (the Holiday Inn has-been singer, the 1994 seaplane crash, the near-divorce) unhinges one's compass, and growth requires disorientation, framed exploration of one's governing assumptions, and re-orientation. She reads the arc of 'Margaritaville' — 'I know it's nobody's fault' to 'hell, it could be my fault' to 'my own damn fault' — as exactly this movement, and Buffett's post-crash fly-fishing for the small bass as embodied, whole-self reflection through which he 'rediscovered his saline psyche.' The chapter's sharpest warning is that escapism is not transformation: the blogger who moved to the beach found that no matter where you go, there you are, because only introspection, not a change of venue, transforms.
- ch. 13 "“When the Coast is Clear”" **·** Immanuel Kant — Perpetual Peace; Cosmopolitanism — Celia Bardwell-Jones asks how Parrothead tourism can be ethical when mass-market tourism walls the Caribbean inside an 'environmental bubble' of consumption — the 'ugly, stupid' tourist of Jamaica Kincaid's Antigua who never encounters the toured other as a fellow agent. Kant's Perpetual Peace sets the standard of hospitality, the stranger's right not to be treated as an enemy, and the chapter asks what duties fall on the traveler in return when tourist industries pressure host cultures 'not to be so damn foreign.' Buffett's novel A Salty Piece of Land supplies the alternative: Tully Mars is saved from free-floating survival when he drops anchor in the relationship with Cleopatra Highbourne — the 'song of the ocean' meeting 'a salty piece of land' — so that escape is redeemed by home, boundary-crossing, and self-reflection with culturally different others.
- ch. 14 "Piratology" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "The Missionary" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Ludwig Wittgenstein, Jean-Paul Sartre, Karl Marx — The Death of God; Authenticity; Existence Precedes Essence; Alienation — Christopher Hoyt reads Buffett's escape from Catholicism as a case study in secular meaning-making after Nietzsche's death of God, taking the Mardi Gras ritual of Folly swatting Death out of town as Buffett's core spiritual attitude — interpreted the way Wittgenstein criticized Frazer, as an expression of our stance toward death rather than mere magic. Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' frames the post-1960s task of self-definition without God, while Marx's alienation explains what the persona of *Jimmy* refuses: the impersonal work and borrowed values that leave moderns living an alien narrative, like McGuane's character Skelton in Ninety-Two in the Shade. The twist is that *Jimmy*'s pop-culture vocabulary — Tully Mars built from Donovan's Reef and Slim Pickens, Bogart, the Brylcreem jingle — is itself authentic, and the 'semi-true story' of the myth tells deeper truths than a literal biography could, making Buffett something like a pop prophet for late modernity.
- ch. 16 "How We Still Might Manage a Smile Being Pirates and Making Meaning" **·** Albert Camus, Friedrich Nietzsche, Socrates — The Absurd; Amor Fati (love of fate); The Unexamined Life — Adam Glover reads 'A Pirate Looks at Forty' through Kristeva's intertextuality: since every text and self is a 'mosaic of quotations' pirated from pre-existing sources, Buffett's confession that he was born 'two hundred years too late' makes him an ironic pirate who can no longer believe or plunder unselfconsciously, unlike the oblivious common-sense pirate. Invoking Barthes's death of the author, he argues the pirate's life is a hard freedom to improvise multiple meanings (the ever-changing 'head uptown' variations in the song) with full responsibility for one's choices. The chapter ends weighing Camus's worry that meaninglessness makes life not worth living against the Nietzsche of The Birth of Tragedy, who answers that the meaning of life is life itself, and it sides with Buffett against Socrates's 'unexamined life' while admitting it cannot settle the question.
- ch. 17 "An Altar Boy’s Public Penance" **·** Baruch Spinoza, Friedrich Nietzsche — The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Substance Monism (Deus sive Natura); Forgiveness — Flamm and Rea take Buffett's altar-boy grudge against Catholic moralism — the 'bakers' of 'Fruitcakes' who try to cure humanity's half-baked madness — and frame it with Nietzsche's charge that 'there was only one Christian, and he died on the cross.' They then cast Buffett as a latter-day Spinoza: like the excommunicated lens-grinder he rejects the orthodox God, finds God in nature ('One Particular Harbor' as a view 'sub specie aeternitatis'), and treats wealth, honor, and sensual pleasure ('Cheeseburger in Paradise') as means toward the greatest happiness rather than sins. Nietzsche's Dionysian intoxication ('God's Own Drunk') and Shakespeare's Sir Toby versus the moralist Malvolio support embracing natural madness, and the chapter closes by arguing Buffett's confessional songs ('Coastal Confessions') make his Parrothead audience the priest who grants the altar boy's public penance and forgiveness.
- ch. 18 "Smart Women and Fruitcakes" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "“Happily Ever After, Now and Then”" **·** Mary Wollstonecraft, Jean-Jacques Rousseau — Feminism; A Vindication of the Rights of Woman; Pragmatism — Erin McKenna explains how a feminist can love Buffett by reading 'Fins' and 'Why Don't We Get Drunk (and Screw)' as critiques of predatory land sharks rather than endorsements, and 'Margaritaville' as a man admitting 'it's my own damn fault.' Against Rousseau's pliable helpmate ideal of woman she sets Wollstonecraft's Vindication — equal education and personhood for women — and Charlotte Perkins Gilman's pragmatist-feminist case that women's economic, physical, and mental dependence stunts everyone. Buffett's novels then pass the Gilman test: Desdemona, Trevor Kane, Cleopatra Highbourne, and Sophie are smart, independent women, and the male leads must reform their habits to earn them, aiming at Desdemona's 'happily ever after, now and then' instead of the fairy-tale ending.
- ch. 20 "The Fruitcake as Performative Exemplar" **·** Judith Butler, Martin Heidegger, John Dewey, Michel Foucault — Gender Performativity; Heteronormativity; The They-Self (das Man) — John Kaag pairs Buffett's 'Fruitcakes' with Judith Butler's constructivism: institutions 'girl' infants through interpellation (the sonogram naming), the heterosexual imperative abjects gay, lesbian, and transgender 'nobodies,' and these excluded fruitcakes are the cosmic baker's half-baked people. The movie-theater stanza ('a twelve pound Nestle Crunch for twenty-five dollars') becomes Heidegger's das Man, others thinking and choosing for us, while Buffett's 'mea culpa' refrain and 'Religion's in the hands of some crazy-ass people' attack the guilt constitutive of Christian subjecthood, with Dewey's broad, doctrine-free religious experience offered as common ground. Buffett concerts themselves are read as performative exemplars — drag-show-like borderland communities where four generations act out the 'little bit of fruitcake' in everyone as a quiet political protest against enforced normalcy.
- ch. 21 "Margarita Metaphysics" *(front)*
- ch. 22 "Wonder Why We Ever Go Home" **·** Communitarianism; Pragmatism; The Golden Rule; The Land Ethic — Duke Richey maps Buffett's West — 'Ringling, Ringling,' the Rancho Deluxe soundtrack, Tully Mars — onto Josiah Royce's philosophy of community: only people who root in a place, face its history ('wise provincialism'), and sacrifice selfish desires for the whole can build Beloved Communities, a lesson enacted when cattle rustlers Jack and Cecil accept community sanction and find belonging working the Rancho Deluxe. Wallace Stegner's coral-reef metaphor from Angle of Repose supplies the image of communities built up millimeter by millimeter yet still vulnerable to pollution and over-fishing, with Royce's environmental regret (covering 'the wounds' of the landscape with gardens) anticipating the chapter's sustainability ethic. 'Wonder Why We Ever Go Home' thus asks what we really seek when we seek grace through community: not the nomadic Pickup Truck Death of every-man-for-himself, but cooperation that makes a society to match the scenery.
- ch. 23 "“Where Did All the Good Songs Go ”" **·** John Dewey — Experience and Education; Pragmatism — Scott Pratt answers whether 'Margaritaville' is art by rejecting object-based theories (Kivy's score-compliance, the abstract perfect performance, the unrecorded instance that vanishes) for Dewey's Art as Experience: art is 'an experience,' complete and self-sufficient, followed by a reflective, evaluative second phase. He reads 'Makin' Music for the Money' as moving from solitary self-interested music-making to a community of musicians, and the Port of Spain steel-drum rehearsal of 'King of Somewhere Hot' that carried forward into the Miami concert as Dewey's two phases in action. Buffett's fly-fishing stories — the lost blue marlin that became 'a story,' the released Long Island bass that 'replenished his saline psyche' — supply Haeckel's ecological model in which music, like fishing, is an organism-environment interaction, making songs 'homemade' eco-music that belongs to listeners in its own ecosystem.
- ch. 24 "“Livin’ and Dyin’ in Three-Quarter Time”" **·** Niccolò Machiavelli, Aristotle — Virtù and Fortuna; Virtue Ethics (arete); The Wheel of Fortune; Fate and Foreknowledge — Randall Auxier uses Buffett's catalog to think about fortune and fate, reading Buffett's bold career moves (walking out on Nashville for the beach, later annexing it via 'It's Five o'Clock Somewhere') through Machiavelli's advice to marry Fortuna and master her tricks with virtù. Against Aristotle's demanding answer that only aretē, moral excellence, defends happiness against bad luck, he takes Vico's middle path: natural causes, moral causes, and the occasions of fortune are gathered under providence, so Buffett's seaplane crash ('God, Buddha, St. Christopher, my guardian angel... luck, and the United States Navy water-survival training') shows any fate can be turned to good ends for others. Sorting Buffett's songs into places, times, meetings, sentiments, and thoughts — the key sentiment being the wistful — the chapter lands on contentment as gratitude: being 'livin' and dyin' in three-quarter time.'
- ch. 25 "Songs Referred to in This Book" *(notes)*
- ch. 26 "Pirates in Paradise" *(notes)*
- ch. 27 "Index" *(notes)*
- ch. 28 "Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 29 "Copyright Page" *(front)*

## Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Johnny Cash and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Dedication" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Introduction" **·** Socrates — The Problem of Evil; Personal Identity — The editors' introduction opens with Socrates on trial for corrupting the youth of Athens and quips that on stage before the youth of Athens, Georgia, Cash could claim he was only asking "What is truth?" It frames Cash as Kris Kristofferson's "walking contradiction" whose paradoxes generate the book's questions: how evil fits a world rated by a benevolent God, where the enduring "I" hides while Cash insisted he was always changing, and what makes a law unjust. It also presents the Man in Black as social critic lobbying officials at San Quentin and Folsom for prison reform and raising money for reservation schools, before welcoming readers with the 1969 Arthur, Illinois concert where hippies and Amish rubbed shoulders.
- ch. 7 "PART I - Self" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "Authentic Cash" **·** Authenticity; Personal Identity — Butler rehearses how the Johnny Cash persona was socially manufactured: Sam Phillips coined the name "Johnny Cash" for its rebellious marketing value, "Folsom Prison Blues" narrates a prison term Cash never served (and borrowed from Jimmie Rodgers and Gordon Jenkins), and the Man in Black image began as an accident of black shirts at a Memphis church performance. Against Jung's persona-as-mask and Dr. Phil's "authentic core self," and armed with George Herbert Mead's social theory of the self, he argues authenticity is not fidelity to a hidden inner essence but active engagement with the social processes shaping one's identity, the way paper money gains "cash value" through use. Cash invested the imposed persona with value by sincerely living it (for example, writing "Man in Black" to give the black clothes his own meaning), so the construct became genuinely his identity.
- ch. 9 "A Modest Conclusion" **·** Personal Identity; Ship of Theseus — Lindahl-Urben and Taliaferro stage the diachronic-versus-episodic debate about the self (Galen Strawson's episodic view included) against Leigh Edwards's "no single Johnny Cash": the hotel-room-wrecking addict and the Billy Graham touring Christian do not fit one biography. They argue the private J.R. was a third option: on stage he becomes wholly absorbed in story characters (the Folsom narrator, the man who shot a man in Reno) while a self not defined by time slips in and out of the persona, evidenced by his account of gradually shedding "Johnny Cash" after shows. Johnny Cash the public quilt is compared to the Ship of Theseus, every original piece of J.R. replaced yet still owned by him, and the modest conclusion is that J.R., like anyone making a free choice, stood above the timeline of instants and could inhabit both the episodes and the grand narrative.
- ch. 10 "I Still Miss Someone The Self and Its Travels Along the Way" **·** Zhuangzi, Laozi, Confucius — The Tao (the Way); Yin and Yang; Taoism (Daoism); Li (ritual propriety) — Geisz explains the Confucian social dao of ritual (li), humaneness (ren), filial piety and the junzi, the Daodejing's metaphysical Dao with its unity of opposites, and Zhuangzi's tales of free wandering, then maps all three onto Cash's songs. Zhuangzi's "Free and Easy Wandering" answers Cash's road songs ("I've Been Everywhere," "The Wanderer"), Cook Ding's effortless carving answers John Henry's hammering in "The Legend of John Henry's Hammer," and the scrambled countdown of "Twenty-Five Minutes to Go" echoes Zhuangzi's logic-bending humor. The payoff is Cash's own country Yin-Yang of interdependent opposites, freedom chained to imprisonment ("Folsom Prison Blues"), sin twinned with redemption ("I Hung My Head"), fidelity with betrayal ("Jackson," "Cocaine Blues"), and a self that, unlike Zhuangzi's self-forgetting sage, must travel a temporal path carrying its guilt, yet stays on what Geisz calls a very wide superhighway of a Dao.
- ch. 11 "PART II - Life" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "If I Were a Carpenter" **·** John Rawls, Immanuel Kant, Hannah Arendt, Aristotle, Socrates — The Veil of Ignorance; The Categorical Imperative; The Golden Rule — Butler asks what makes an activity work, testing the market definition against Socrates' refusal of fees, Aristotle's Politics, Arendt's labor/work/action distinction, Eva Kittay's care work, and the split between extrinsic and intrinsic value. He reads Cash's catalog through it: "One Piece at a Time" (the Detroit line worker stealing a Cadillac he builds but cannot afford), "Get Rhythm" (the shoeshine boy singing through menial labor), "I Never Picked Cotton" (escaping work into an empty identity), "Let Him Roll" and "Southern Accents," and the San Quentin monologue after "Wreck of the Ol' 97" where Cash refuses to be told what to play before inmates. The chapter closes by lining up Kant's categorical imperative, Jesus' Golden Rule, and Rawls's veil of ignorance: nobody would choose a society of company-store wage slavery without knowing they were not the worker, and Cash, knowing he stood on the stage rather than in the cellblock, used his freedom to side with prisoners and carpenters anyway.
- ch. 13 "What Is Truth" **·** John Locke, Aristotle — Democracy — Lavaque-Manty and Mickey define populism by distinguishing its content from its discourse (via Michael Kazin), tracing the 1892 Populist Party platform and southern race-baiting demagogues like Vardaman and Huey Long, then locate Cash in that Dixie soil, his family rescued by the patronizing New Deal Dyess Colony that fed his populist distrust of elites. Cash's populism is anti-racist and pro-prisoner ("The Ballad of Ira Hayes," his empathy for convicts against tough-on-crime politics), his patriotism borders on kitsch ("Ragged Old Flag"), and "What Is Truth?" argues the young may be right, breaking with populist certainty about the obvious. The closing worry is the deep tension they pose with Locke's "the people be the judge" against democracy as "government by discussion": a Cash concert, like a mass rally, may stir people following rather than thinking, so populism's ring of truth is not yet truth.
- ch. 14 "Love Gone Good" **·** Paul Tillich, Jean-Paul Sartre, Socrates, Friedrich Nietzsche — Radical Freedom and Responsibility; Philosophy of Love — Johnson reads Cash as practicing "philosophy as a way of life" rather than theorizing: his love-gone-bad songs ("Cocaine Blues," "I shot a man in Reno," the addictions he chose) honor the descent into darkness, aligned with Socrates going down to Piraeus in the Republic, Nietzsche's Zarathustra descending into the depths, and biblical descents from Jacob at the Jabbok to Jonah to Christ, while his love-gone-good songs ("Daddy Sang Bass," "Man in Black") show the turn outward through which love interrupts darkness without erasing it. He frames this with Gabriel Marcel's "creative fidelity" (being at the disposal of others), Paul Tillich's courage to be, in which love is stronger than the nonbeing of death, and Sartre's Existentialism Is a Humanism, where wanting my freedom obligates me to want everyone's. The Man in Black thus carries "a little darkness" on his back while insisting "all God's children ain't free," a lived, political-ethical philosophy rather than a doctrine.
- ch. 15 "John Henry, the Steam-Engine, and Folsom Prisoners" **·** John Stuart Mill — Higher and Lower Pleasures; The Greatest Happiness Principle; On Liberty; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Mulnix pairs Cash with John Stuart Mill on the priority of quality of life over mere life: Mill's 1868 Parliament speech defends capital punishment as more humane than the "living tomb" of life imprisonment, and Cash agrees in the Folsom liner notes (the prisoner envying the cockroach that can leave) and in "The Mercy Seat," where the electric chair becomes both mercy and the throne of God. Mill's higher and lower pleasures, competent judges, and On Liberty's individuality illuminate Cash's gallery of fools, the "Folsom Prison Blues" narrator who shot a man just to watch him die, the mother-defying Billy Joe of "Don't Take Your Guns to Town," characters whose unreflective rebellion squanders rational freedom. John Henry, by contrast, exercised his higher faculties against the steam-engine and so died happy, proving the chapter's Millian thesis that freedom matters as a means to self-directed, deliberated happiness.
- ch. 16 "PART III - Love" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "Conclusion June Love Beyond the Jordan" **·** Harry Frankfurt, Immanuel Kant — Philosophy of Love; Humanity as an End in Itself — Sennett builds "June Love" out of June Carter Cash's documented love, from the "Hurt" video's staircase glance to Rosanne Cash's eulogy that June saw your potential and "lifted them up" for you to see, and the love that steadied John through addictions and infidelity for thirty-five years. He stages the philosophy-of-love dilemma between appraisal theories (Velleman, grounding love in Kantian dignity that demands respect but cannot justify loving John rather than anyone) and bestowal theories (Irving Singer, on which love projects value and so cannot be justified at all), with Frankfurt's volitional account as a side note, and proposes June Love, loving the beloved's potentiality, as the hybrid that is both objective and active and can justify loving this person. He also distinguishes June Love from codependence: enabling entrenches the addict's destruction, whereas June's confronting-and-encouraging love, echoed in "Ring of Fire" and "Far Side Banks of Jordan," called Cash to transformation while leaving him himself.
- ch. 18 "And Beware of the Beast in Me" **·** Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Barnes takes Cash's infidelity despite the pledged fidelity of "I Walk the Line" and refuses the easy diagnoses of hypocrisy or lying: "Guess Things Happen that Way" voices a good will overcome by weakness, a frail human nature anyone shares. He supports this with the situationist experiments, the dime in the pay-phone slot, the Princeton seminarians in a hurry, Milgram's obedient schoolteachers, and the Stanford prison simulation that turned a pacifist student into an abusive guard, showing situation outweighs character. From Cash's songs he draws two moral lessons: charity toward wrongdoers, since the man in "I Never Picked Cotton" or the drunkard of "Kneeling Drunkard's Plea" might be us under the same circumstances, and prudence about compromising situations, as when Billy Joe's fatal pride in "Don't Take Your Guns to Town" proves his mother right.
- ch. 19 "The Doors Are Never Locked" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Augustine of Hippo — Forgiveness; Eternal Recurrence; Master and Slave Morality; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Held reads Cash's Walk the Line retort "Well, they're not Christians then" as a thesis about redemption: since, with Augustine, we rejoice most at the sinner saved, and since the Sermon on the Mount forbids judging what we cannot know (anyone's deep character), humility demands withholding condemnation and hoping even the worst can change. He contrasts Christian redemption, a revaluation of the person that needs outside grace (Cash needed June and the Carters; nobody is self-made), with Nietzsche's attack on redemption as slave-morality self-hatred, granting that Nietzsche's eternal recurrence also revalues the past but objecting that self-revaluation collapses into rationalization, as Cash's Saul in Man in White shows. Forgiveness proper requires repentance and a solvent character, like paying off a debt; the shame of the "Long Black Veil" woman shows why; and because we see "through a glass darkly," nobody, not the Reno murderer, not Joe Bean, is beyond hope, which is why the doors are never locked and why execution or life without parole claims a judgment of moral worth that is not ours to make.
- ch. 20 "From Cash to Kant—and Back Again" **·** Immanuel Kant — Kingdom of Ends; The Categorical Imperative; Humanity as an End in Itself; The Golden Rule — Yolanda Estes pairs Cash with Kant as two duty-based moralists: Cash's Golden Rule in 'The Preacher Said, Jesus Said' parallels Kant's formula of humanity (never treating persons merely as means), and Cash's 'good heart' matches Kant's good will, since songs like 'Sam Hall,' 'Folsom Prison Blues' (the man shot in Reno 'just to watch him die'), and 'I Hung My Head' weigh inner motives over outcomes. Because earthly law never balances the moral scale, she reads Kant's kingdom of ends and Cash's apocalyptic kingdom of God in 'When the Man Comes Around' and 'God's Gonna Cut You Down' as parallel objects of faith: we must live as if perfect justice already prevails, working to improve this world rather than waiting for the next.
- ch. 21 "PART IV - Justice" *(front)*
- ch. 22 "The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly" **·** John Stuart Mill, Socrates — Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; Utilitarianism; The Harm Principle — Johnson and Schmitz argue that Cash, through songs like 'San Quentin,' 'Jacob Green,' and his cover of 'The Mercy Seat,' championed reforming prisons from a retributive to a rehabilitative model and abolishing capital punishment (songs like 'Joe Bean' and 'Long Black Veil' center executed innocents). They defend Cash with Mill: Socrates shows vengeful retributive sentiment is immoral, Mill's harm principle says government may coerce only to prevent harm, so punishment should be justified only by future deterrence and rehabilitation. Since the death penalty's deterrent effect is empirically weak (California, Missouri-vs-Iowa murder rates) and wrongful convictions are common, Mill today would join Cash in calling for abolition.
- ch. 23 "“Unchained” The Inspired Anger of a Religious Man" **·** Aristotle, Plato, Thomas Aquinas — The Golden Mean; Intentionality; Virtue Ethics (arete) — Dan Haggerty uses Aristotle's account of anger as a virtuous mean—felt at the right people, time, and degree—to show that songs like 'San Quentin,' 'The Man in Black,' and 'Oney' express justified anger at real injustices done to prisoners and workingmen, contra pop psychology's blanket rejection of anger. He then coins 'inspired anger' (drawing on Plato's Ion: the artist possessed and blown away by emotion): a painful, hopeless desire for a justice or restoration that can never be, exemplified by Cash's 'Hurt' video and its regret over irrecoverable time—mourning rather than self-pity or depression. The chapter closes with 'Unchained' as a prayer showing how a Christian like Cash can live with this futile desire rather than argue it away.
- ch. 24 "What Is Justice" **·** John Rawls, Plato, Mahatma Gandhi — The Veil of Ignorance; Justice as Fairness; Justice in the Republic — Johnny Huss extracts multiple theories of justice from 'Jacob Green'—desert (traced to Plato's Republic), equal treatment, conventionalism, and systemic injustice—and argues that desert collapses once responsibility is pushed back to factors beyond our control (Cash's God-given voice, the 'victim of the times'). Rawls's veil of ignorance supplies the standard for judging institutions: since anyone could be Jacob Green, we could not accept principles that let anyone 'get done like Jacob Green got done.' The chapter extends this to social justice for Native Americans via 'The Ballad of Ira Hayes' and 'As Long as the Grass Shall Grow,' including the flooded Cornplanter Tract, and closes insisting justice requires action, not just principles.
- ch. 25 "PART V - God" *(front)*
- ch. 26 "Memories Are Made of This" **·** Plato, Plutarch, Aristotle — Personal Identity; Ship of Theseus; Personal Identity (memory theory); Immortality and the Soul — Randall Jensen asks whether Cash's hope of reunion with the dead ('Meet Me in Heaven,' 'If We Never Meet Again This Side of Heaven') is even coherent, using the 'One Piece at a Time' Cadillac and a hypothetical 1954 Plymouth to retell the Ship of Theseus puzzle about identity through part replacement. He canvasses Platonic dualism from the Phaedo (Cash is his soul, the body a rusty cage), the materialist hope that God can reassemble a resurrected body despite dispersed matter, and the psychological-continuity view that persons are 'made of memories,' ending on the duplication problem: if God made two heavenly bodies both carrying Cash's memories, which one would be Cash?
- ch. 27 "Redemption" **·** Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas — Virtue Ethics (arete); The Problem of Evil; Cardinal and Theological Virtues — Stephen Bilynskyj tests John Hick's soul-making theodicy—that God allows suffering because virtues like courage, temperance, and compassion need pain to form—against Cash's life and songs. Using Aristotle on habituation by pleasure and pain (Cash's first amphetamine euphoria and the ostrich-attack painkillers as missed occasions for temperance) and Aquinas on innate aptitude and divinely infused virtue, he argues virtue can form without suffering (by genes or miracle), so soul-making alone cannot justify evil, as Cash himself implies about his mother's grief after Jack's death. Cash instead locates redemption in Christ's suffering ('Redemption,' 'Why Me, Lord?'), while the intervention by his son John Carter shows pain still occasioning real growth in temperance.
- ch. 28 "“A Boy Named Sue” A Cashian Theodicy" **·** Augustine of Hippo, Gottfried Leibniz, Plato — The Problem of Evil; The Divided Will; The Best of All Possible Worlds — Jamie Carlin Watson reads Cash's Christian worldview as Augustinian: evil is not a positive substance but a privation or corruption of good (contra the monism Leibniz risks and the Manichean dualism Augustine rejected), so humans alone bear blame for moral evil through freely corrupting good things—'Cocaine Blues,' 'The Wall,' the Folsom prisoner who admits he 'had it coming,' and the divided self of 'The Beast in Me' echoing Romans 7. Natural evil, as in 'Guess Things Happen That Way' and the flood of 'Five Feet High and Rising' (Cash's mother's 'blessing' of rich river dirt), serves punishment or greater goods. 'A Boy Named Sue' dramatizes the residual tension: the father's get-tough-or-die theodicy convinces neither Sue nor us that the sheer amount of evil is justified.
- ch. 29 "Christmas in Jamaica" **·** Alvin Plantinga, David Hume, Epicurus, Thomas Aquinas — The Problem of Evil; Compatibilism; Free Will vs Determinism — David Werther frames Jack Cash's saw death—which Cash told Nick Tosches he considered murder—and the 1982 armed robbery at Cinnamon Hill as tests of Epicurus's old questions (quoted via Hume): could a good, powerful God have prevented these evils? Distinguishing the evidential from the logical problem, he answers the logical problem with Plantinga's libertarian free will: not even God could ensure Cash freely 'walked the line' with Vivian, since guaranteeing fidelity would eliminate freedom. He rebuts the compatibilist counterobjection by arguing, with Aquinas, that nothing can be the cause of its own nature, and argues heaven can still fulfill Johnny and June's hope of meeting 'on the far side banks of the Jordan' even if the redeemed can no longer act wrongly.

## Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Led Zeppelin and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Foreword" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Acknowledgments" *(notes)*
- ch. 7 "And If You Listen Very Hard . ." **·** Aristotle — Editor Scott Calef's introduction argues that the critics who dismissed Led Zeppelin as hype, blues thieves, and purveyors of mere excess were wrong: Page and Jones had long apprenticeships, Plant spread asphalt while struggling, and the band released four albums in two years while touring nonstop. It contends the band invites philosophy because Page (occultism, the Hermit tarot figure on Led Zeppelin IV) and Plant (mythology, the feather-of-truth symbol) were serious spiritual seekers, and because Zep's music resists tidy genre categories just as philosophy challenges our everyday categories of creativity, recognition, and value. It closes by invoking Aristotle's claim that philosophy begins in wonder, prompted by Plant's 'it makes me wonder' in 'Stairway to Heaven'.
- ch. 8 "From Low to High Culture Where’s That Confounded Bridge" **·** Immanuel Kant — Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — John Stone-Mediatore argues that Led Zeppelin's music, especially in concert, is a quintessential experience of the sublime. He applies Burke's catalogue of sublime qualities (loudness, darkness, rudeness, the artificial infinite) to Bonham's cavernous drum sound on 'When the Levee Breaks', Page's rough overdriven tone and 'sloppy' technique, and the dissonant mandolin intro and nocturnal imagery of 'The Battle of Evermore'; Longinus's inspired, thunderbolt-like genius explains Plant's overnight writing of the 'Stairway to Heaven' lyrics at Headley Grange. Kant's account of imagination, understanding, and reason then shows why the impossible stairway to heaven, 'our shadows taller than our soul', and 'when all are one and one is all' frustrate concepts and delight us through reason's superiority. The chapter concludes that once rock attains the sublime, the high/low culture distinction is mere aesthetic snobbery.
- ch. 9 "Bring It On Home to You" **·** Andy Clark, Plato, Immanuel Kant — The Extended Mind; Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Jeanette Bicknell argues that the two classic models of creativity—Plato's Ion, where the rhapsode is a divinely possessed conduit, and Kant's solitary genius who issues new rules—cannot explain a four-piece rock band, since both are individualistic, purely mental, and end in mystery. Her positive account uses Clark and Chalmers's extended mind (Page describes his guitar as 'an extension of you', instruments and notation as cognitive props) and Keith Sawyer's collaborative emergence: Zeppelin's creativity happened in rehearsal and performance, as with the stairwell-recorded drum groove of 'When the Levee Breaks' that framed every later musical decision. The transformation of Joan Baez's 'Babe, I'm Gonna Leave You' into a whisper-to-cry hard-rock template shows the band creating something no member could have produced or predicted alone.
- ch. 10 "Authentic Rock" **·** Immanuel Kant — Authenticity; Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Theodore Gracyk asks whether Zeppelin's uncredited borrowings—Willie Dixon's 'You Need Love' into 'Whole Lotta Love', Spirit's 'Taurus' into 'Stairway to Heaven', Jake Holmes's 'I'm Confused' into 'Dazed and Confused'—undermine their status as an authentic rock band whose value supposedly rests on sincere self-expression and original songwriting. Using Hanslick's thought experiment as staged by Little Roger and the Goosebumps's 'Gilligan's Island (Stairway)' parody and Handel's recycling of his own music into the Messiah, he argues a song's expressive power comes from the interaction of words and music (guarding against the fallacies of division and composition), and that by itself music is neither angry nor spiritual. Since Zeppelin's instrumental arrangements diverge radically from their sources and the lawsuits turned on Plant's lyrics, the chapter concludes that transformation, not narrow originality, grounds their genius—so the rock-versus-pop authenticity standard must be loosened.
- ch. 11 "Tell Me No Lies, Make Me a Happy Man" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Martin Heidegger, Arthur Schopenhauer — Intentionality; Phenomenology — Luke Dick gives a phenomenological analysis of what it is to be moved by 'Black Dog', introducing affectivity through a fantasy in which a stranger insulting Zeppelin instantly provokes anger. Sartre's account of emotions as unreflective, 'magical' transformations directed at intentional objects explains how fast the insulted fan's world changes, while Heidegger's claim that we are never moodless grounds the idea of a distinct 'Zeppelin mood' that the band's sound articulates better than language could. Schopenhauer's misogynist essay 'On Women' is set beside the song's predatory canine sexuality, and the chapter ends by asking which of the three 'males'—Schopenhauer, Plant's character, or the author with his carefully chosen six-song mix CD—a father could endorse as a son-in-law.
- ch. 12 "I’m Gonna Crawl" **·** Karl Marx — Objectification; Commodity Fetishism — Richard Wilson and Emma Rees apply Freud's theory of fetishism—the boy's disavowal of castration displaced onto a substitute object—to Zeppelin's lyrics and imagery. 'Trampled Underfoot' continues Robert Johnson's 'Terraplane Blues' car-as-lover convention, 'Custard Pie' and 'Black Dog' turn women into consumable food (Freud's cannibalistic pregenital sexual organization), and 'The Lemon Song' and 'Whole Lotta Love' avert the castrating vagina, with the Seattle red snapper episode read through the vagina dentata myth. The band's misogyny ('Soul of a woman was created below' in 'Dazed and Confused', echoing Lear), the voyeuristic die-cut windows of the Physical Graffiti cover, and Plant's cock-rock persona in The Song Remains the Same all illustrate how fetishistic substitution neutralizes the threatening female body and explains the band's compulsive doomed-relationship songs; the authors briefly borrow Marx's language of commodification for the woman-car-drugs as status objects.
- ch. 13 "Singing of the Good Things" **·** Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Socrates, John Locke, Thomas Hobbes — Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society; The State of Nature; Free Will vs Determinism — Scott Calef asks whether Led Zeppelin's lives of wealth, groupies, and no-questions-asked liberty were genuinely free and therefore enviable. Locke's distinction between weak freedom (doing what you want, with Page happily locked in his suite at the Riot House) and strong freedom (being able to do otherwise, defended via beer-spilling concert excuses) is destabilized by the observation that no one ever does other than what they did. Rousseau then dominates: the state of nature versus LA, freedom as the capacity to resist natural impulse, which explains both Zep's libertine promiscuity and the paradox that heroin and alcohol enslave the very freedom that took them (the post-Physical Graffiti decline, Bonzo's death), while the band's violence—Bonham's assaults, the Oakland beating—shows society's suppression of natural pity, not natural aggression as Hobbes would have it. Socrates gets the last word: doing what we please is not doing what we truly want, so only the temperate person is free.
- ch. 14 "True Selves Found or Made" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Arthur Schopenhauer — Existence Precedes Essence; Second-Order Desires (personhood); Free Will vs Determinism — Theodore Schick reconstructs Aleister Crowley's philosophy of Thelema to explain Jimmy Page's devotion—Boleskine Manor, The Equinox bookstore, the Zoso sigil, 'Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the law' etched in Led Zeppelin III's run-out groove—and reads 'Stairway to Heaven' stanza by stanza as an allegory of awakening to the True Will. He then dismantles the framework: no spell has ever worked under controlled conditions (post hoc fallacy), Sartre's existence precedes essence denies any divinely written True Will or human nature, and Schopenhauer (via Einstein) argues we can do what we want but cannot want what we want. Using second-order desires and autonomy, the chapter concludes that selves are made, not found—so even if a True Will existed, following a program we did not write would make us 'loyal plastic robots', not free.
- ch. 15 "As We Wind on Down the Road" **·** The Rhizome — Randall Auxier develops a theory, drawn from Ernst Cassirer's work on myth and magic, that distinguishes magic (the generalizing of will so that past, present, and future connect through symbols and co-operating forces) from myth (the consciousness that experiences the world as wills and archetypal symbols). Page embodies the magical path—the zone musicians enter where playing exceeds conscious control, the Faustian need to master it that led him to Crowley, and the risk of being drained (Page in 1977)—while Plant embodies myth, supplying archetypal lyrics ('The Battle of Evermore', 'Kashmir', 'Stairway' as 'a song of hope') and the Welsh pastoral. Zeppelin's blues borrowing is re-enactment rather than repetition, a rhizome-like reinvention of old roots, and the four unpronounceable symbols of the fourth album are genuine creations: symbols that store concentrated will for the future.
- ch. 16 "I Ain’t Gonna Tell You One Thing that You Really Ought to Know . . . Ooh!" **·** Plato, René Descartes, Martin Heidegger, David Hume, Socrates, Ludwig Wittgenstein — Theory of Forms; Bundle Theory of Self; Being-Toward-Death; Immortality and the Soul — Scott Calef reads the black 'Object' on the Presence cover—which Storm Thorgerson calls not a presence but a hole—to argue that absence permeates Zep's album art (the cut-out wheel of III, the die-cut windows of Physical Graffiti, the spindle holes of Coda) and that holes are a genuine metaphysical puzzle: immaterial yet extended, seemingly causal, and hard to see on a causal theory of perception. Descartes's immaterial soul is compared to holes (both non-physical, though holes suspiciously have size and location), Plato's Forms explain how the Object and we ourselves partake of both Being and Non-Being, and Hume's failure to find a self in introspection makes the self 'a hole'. Kierkegaard and Heidegger connect nothingness to the anxiety of death—fitting an album made after Plant's near-fatal crash—Socrates's two alternatives about death frame the end, and Wittgenstein's 'not a something but not a nothing either' caps the Object's dual nature.
- ch. 17 "Close the Door, Put Out the Lights" **·** Immanuel Kant, Aristotle — Utilitarianism; The Categorical Imperative; The Golden Mean; Humanity as an End in Itself — Scott Calef tests three ethical theories against Led Zeppelin's off-stage destruction: TV-tossing, samurai-slashed hotel rooms, food fights, sharks hung in closets at the Edgewater Inn, the red snapper incident, and Jimmy Page's relationship with fourteen-year-old Lori Maddox. Classical utilitarianism weighs Bonzo's glee against the traumatized chambermaid, displaced guests, and unpaid-for sleep loss, generally condemning the pranks while leaving the supposedly consensual snapper episode uncomfortably open. Kant condemns across the board: Plant's fake tour itineraries and the stolen 'Black Beauty' Les Paul fail the universalizability test, trashing hotel rooms is self-defeating when universalized, and treating the Portland woman as a mere means violates her dignity as a rational agent; Aristotle's golden mean finds the band's excess nowhere near virtue, whatever Caligula would say. The chapter closes by separating moral judgment of the men from appreciation of the music.
- ch. 18 "Coda" **·** Plutarch, Aristotle, John Locke — Ship of Theseus; Personal Identity — Gimbel asks what makes a band remain the same band over time: Led Zeppelin survived replacing drummer John Bonham with his son Jason, yet Page and Jones insist no singer could replace Robert Plant. Working through Plutarch's Ship of Theseus, Aristotle's essential properties, and Locke's continuity account of identity, he uses Peter French's distinction between aggregates (groups defined by membership) and conglomerates (defined by role structure) to argue a band is a conglomerate. The twist is that a reunion would be a monument like Theseus's preserved ship rather than a working vessel: Plant is an Aristotelian essential of what Zeppelin was, while Jason Bonham's family link supplies the reverence and facsimile-fidelity a monument needs.
- ch. 19 "When the Levee Breaks Excess as Truth" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Arthur Schopenhauer, Heraclitus — The Apollonian and the Dionysian; The World as Will; Everything Flows / Logos — Flynn reads the Swan Song logo (Rimmer's falling Apollo) and songs like 'Kashmir,' 'Whole Lotta Love,' and 'When the Levee Breaks' through Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy: individuals are temporary manifestations of a chaotic primordial unity (Schopenhauer's will), and Dionysian art redeems that suffering by celebrating the very excess that undoes us. The sandstorm of 'Kashmir,' the relentless sexual longing of the traveling blues, Plant's death-moan-as-ecstasy in 'In My Time of Dying,' and Bonham's levee-crushing drums all enact 'excess revealed as truth' — joyous laments in which words bleed into music. This is not hedonism, Flynn argues, but ecstatic awareness that the self's boundaries are artificial and its dissolution is a kind of reunion.
- ch. 20 "Bring the Balance Back Led Zeppelin and the Hegelian Dialectic" **·** G.W.F. Hegel — The Dialectic; Geist (World Spirit); History Has a Direction — Macan argues Zeppelin's contradictions — 'cock rock' versus androgyny, blues versus avant-garde sound collages, acoustic versus electric, East versus West — are Hegelian dualities driven toward monist synthesis by a World-Spirit working through the band's generation. He reads the physical riff sections and shadowy middle collages of 'Dazed and Confused' and 'Whole Lotta Love' as interpenetrating Primitive/Modern, African-American/European, and Male/Female poles; 'Stairway to Heaven''s seamless growth from recorder-and-lute evocations of Elizabethan England into full hard rock reconciles past and present (via Tolkien, the Hermit gatefold, the Lady and the Piper); and 'Kashmir' versus 'In the Light' stage Jung's East/West problem, with Crowley's Schopenhauerian will supplying the turn from wisdom sought without to wisdom found within.
- ch. 21 "Led Zeppelin and Art" **·** G.W.F. Hegel — Struggle for Recognition; Master–Slave Dialectic — Shain uses Hegel's master-slave dialectic and the struggle for recognition to explain the band: Page and Jones formed Zeppelin because recognition as top session players wasn't enough, and the drive for critic and peer recognition — which varied by hierarchy, as when Bonham said 'If Buddy Rich says I'm shit, then I'm shit' — pushed the band from the bombastic early albums to the achievement of Led Zeppelin IV and Physical Graffiti. Recognition extends to groupies (association and gratification, sharpening feminism's empowerment-versus-objectification dilemma about Des Barres) and to the high-art question: claims like 'Stairway as landmark artistic achievement of the twentieth century' misfire, Shain argues, because using high-art elements such as improvisation or minimalism can simply make better pop culture without lifting Zeppelin into the art tradition.
- ch. 22 "Sneaking In through the Back Door" **·** Walter Benjamin — The Aura of the Artwork — Seng asks whether The Song Remains the Same can relive the concert experience, using Benjamin's account of the artwork's aura. The ritual of queuing for tickets, the stable set list, Plant's city shout-outs (compared to Homer's rhapsodes naming local warriors), and Page's unrepeatable improvisations give each show a unique aura, while recording 'pries the event from its shell,' makes experiences interchangeable, and turns viewers into 'absent-minded examiners' who judge by price and camera angle. He concedes the movie's camera angles may open new appreciation unavailable even from a Garden seat, but insists being there is a different kind of experience no DVD duplicates.
- ch. 23 "Coda" **·** John Locke — Labor Theory of Property; Utilitarianism — White asks whether fans who trade or sell Led Zeppelin bootlegs wrong the band, given how little official live material it released. He weighs Locke's labor-mixing account of property (the band creates the performance, but tapers 'mix their labor' too), the legal view of property as a bundle of rights, and rule-utilitarian arguments that bootlegs promote the band without cutting into sales of studio albums. He concludes with Ronald Dworkin's point that rights trump utility: if the live performance is the band's property, the band's choice to withhold it binds fans whatever happiness wider distribution would produce.
- ch. 24 "Is Led Zeppelin, after All, the Most Philosophical of Rock Bands" **·** Gilles Deleuze, Friedrich Nietzsche, Immanuel Kant — The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Surber asks why we really listen to Zeppelin when the lyrics carry no philosophy. Kant's Critique of Judgment ranked music lowest among the arts — a 'mere play of sound sensations' at the zero point of philosophy — while Nietzsche reversed him by rooting philosophy in Dionysian rhythm; Deleuze's 'surface' philosophy (height, depth, surfaces; flows, intensities, blockages, repetition-with-difference) then resolves the question. Zeppelin enacts the bodily surface flow — 'Stairway''s gradual build, the flow-blockage-new-flow segues of the 25-minute 'Dazed and Confused' on How the West Was Won, Plant dropping lyrics to use his voice as an instrument — syncing us with lived experience, which makes them the most philosophical of rock bands precisely without saying anything philosophical.
- ch. 25 "Many Times I’ve Wondered 77 Zep Facts, Anecdotes, and Trivia" *(no index entry yet)* — A back-matter list of 77 facts and anecdotes: chart trivia, album-cover stories, rival readings of the four runic symbols (Saturn/666 versus Thor's hammer), Page's Crowley and Lucifer Rising connections, bootleg history, and touring debauchery. It advances no philosophical argument of its own but supplies background the essays draw on, such as the occult symbolism behind the magic chapters and the Willie Dixon credit behind 'Whole Lotta Love.'
- ch. 26 "Top Eleven Contributor Top Ten Lists" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Arthur Schopenhauer, Immanuel Kant — The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Eleven contributor top-ten lists, several applying the book's philosophical tools in miniature: Stone-Mediatore ranks ten songs by how they exemplify Burke's, Kant's, and Longinus's theories of the sublime ('Stairway to Heaven' first), Flynn ranks ten by Nietzsche's Dionysian criterion of celebrating the natural forces that undo us ('When the Levee Breaks' first), and Dick pairs ten songs with Schopenhauer's misogynist essay 'On Women.' The remaining lists — resources, sideman appearances, cover versions, oral fixations, gigs attended — are fanzine fare without philosophical content.

## Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Martial Arts and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Popular Culture and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Fighting Talk" **·** Socrates, Plato, Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Buddhism; Stoicism; Utilitarianism — The editors' introduction argues that philosophy and fighting have been companions since Socrates the soldier and Plato the wrestler (whose name means 'broad shouldered' from the gym), and that each can illuminate the other. It tours the volume through concrete cases: budo courtesy drawn from Shinto, Confucianism and Zen; the Shaolin monks' exercises as a route to Buddhahood; Western chivalry and Gordon Marino's boxing as educations in Aristotelian courage; fencing's egoism and value; and the Stoicism of karate and utilitarianism of Kano's judo. Philosophy clarifies fighting traditions, while fights supply puzzles for ethics, aesthetics, and the philosophy of mind.
- ch. 6 "Enter the Dragon - Traditional Asian Martial Arts" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Free Your Mind, and Your Roundhouse Will Follow" **·** Aristotle, Confucius, The Buddha — Ren (benevolence/humaneness); Li (ritual propriety); Virtue Ethics (arete); Zen Buddhism — Young argues that dojo courtesy is not the fantasy that good manners win fights (Napoleon and the Karate Kid's Johnny lost on skill, not rudeness) but the framing of a craft within a way of life. He maps Aristotle's techne/ethos distinction onto the Japanese jutsu/do pairing to show founders like Kano, Funakoshi and Ueshiba treated fighting as one part of a whole ethical character, reads his seiza apology to an injured yellow belt through Confucian ren, li, yi and shu, and traces Shinto purity into the sincerity (kime) of committed sparring. His black-belt humiliation by seniors becomes Zen's 'courtesy of brutal': ego-deflating violence that trains no-mindedness (muga, Takuan Soho's fudoshin).
- ch. 8 "2 - An Interview with Bodhidharma" **·** The Buddha — Zen Buddhism; Non-Self (anatman); Emptiness (sunyata); Compassion (karuna) — Priest stages a spoof radio interview with Bodhidharma at the Shaolin Temple to argue that the monks' fighting exercises are really meditation: a fist passing an inch from your nose focuses the mind, and repeatedly practicing violent techniques makes practitioners less violent. Bodhidharma explains that a liter of goat's milk, a marauding thug, and even the reporter's self are only conceptual labels over 'thusness' (tathata), that attachment and the desire to strike cause suffering to the striker, and that the Buddha's compassion permits self-defense without aggression. The punchline is the reporter's unanswered last question: 'They're not really about fighting, are they?'
- ch. 9 "A Koan" **·** Zen Buddhism — Finnigan and Tanaka use the kendo student Kenzo, struck down whenever he thinks 'Now is the time to strike!', to pose the puzzle of intentional action without thought. They set Donald Davidson's causal theory of action (intentions as belief-desire causes) against Takuan Soho's mushin, which warns that wherever you put your mind it stops, then resolve it: training lets a master act 'as Yagyu would', and giving reasons afterwards is how one accepts responsibility for an action no reason was 'in mind' for. The koan dissolves once how-questions (how could I act without thinking?) are distinguished from why-questions (why did you do that?).
- ch. 10 "And the Winner Is" **·** Plato, The Buddha — Tripartite Soul; Non-Self (anatman); The Philosopher King; Zen Buddhism — Lynch pits Plato against the Shaolin monks on the nature of the self that martial training is supposed to master. Plato's Republic makes the athlete-warrior Guardian a harmonious, rationally ruled tripartite soul whose bravery is 'remembering what ought and ought not to be feared', trained so reason governs aggression; Buddhism instead dissolves the self into five impermanent aggregates (illustrated by the chariot analogy) and reads mushin as a direct taste of no-self. He awards the practical decision to the Buddhist fighting monks, since no-self explains martial spontaneity and naturally arising compassion, while admitting Plato's substantive rational soul is not strictly refuted.
- ch. 11 "Knowledge and Mastery" *(no index entry yet)* — Schubert asks what his own master's certificate actually certified and dismantles two accounts of martial mastery: the 'Secret Knowledge' account (hidden teachings like Crouching Tiger's stolen Wu Dan manual) and the 'Complete Knowledge' account, which absurdly implies mastery is suspended when a new takedown joins the syllabus or his forgetful Iaido master omits a step of a form. Using the distinction between knowing-that, knowing-how and physical ability (he knew how to jump-spin heel-kick with his foot in a cast), he argues mastery is knowing that and how across the essential techniques, principles and strategies a style could have consisted of, by analogy with fluency in a language. Rank, politics and even the ability to perform are at best signs of mastery, not the thing itself.
- ch. 12 "The Karate Kid - Character and Education" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "An Enemy Lying in Ambush" **·** Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius, Zeno of Citium, Seneca — Stoicism; The Dichotomy of Control — Fuller reads his teenage collapse while holding shiko dachi at his Eighth Kyu grading as a weakness of will, and argues that karate is Stoic discipline embodied. He explains the dichotomy of control through Epictetus's barbecue etiquette and the Kill Bill II buried-alive scene (only the Bride's years of disciplined training, not magic, break the coffin), then lays out living according to nature, Zeno's apatheia, Marcus Aurelius's Meditations, and Seneca's nightly self-examination as the model of askesis. Kata becomes 'a defiant stand against irrational emotion-chasing', and since only virtue is up to us, the enemy 'lying in ambush' is always internal: ourselves.
- ch. 14 "Don’t Carry the World upon Your Shoulders. Only Your Opponent" **·** Jeremy Bentham, John Stuart Mill — Utilitarianism; The Greatest Happiness Principle; The Hedonic Calculus — Cooper and Taylor argue that Kano's judo principles, seiryokuzenyou (maximum efficiency) and jitakyouei (mutual welfare and benefit), echo Bentham's principle of utility: both men swept away archaic rules to reach one efficient ethical goal, and Kano accepted the comparison. They run the hedonic calculus over training bruises versus the joy of a clean throw, use Mill's secondary principles as rule-utilitarian guidelines (release the armbar at the tap rather than calculating each time), and answer the objection that utilitarianism demands too much with Kano's own ethos: like judo, it is about continual improvement, not impossible maximization.
- ch. 15 "Living the Absurd Life" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Friedrich Nietzsche — Existentialism; Existence Precedes Essence; The Absurd; Authenticity — Krein asks why he has spent fifteen years on karate when pepper spray and avoidance would serve self-defense better, and answers with existentialism rather than Buddhism. Nietzsche's death of God and Sartre's claim that existence precedes essence leave life objectively meaningless, but the dojo supplies a self-contained standard for Sartrean transcendence (kata quality is judged within the art), trains the courage and clarity authenticity requires, and enforces excuse-free responsibility: in sparring you either score or you don't. Studying a traditional martial art is thus a heroic, 'act without hope' defiance of the absurd.
- ch. 16 "The Last Resort" **·** Michel Foucault — Feminism; Power/Knowledge — Petersen recounts fighting off a man who threatened to rape and kill her, and argues that karate, not feminist doctrine or therapy, made her a real feminist by rewiring her self-concept, fear responses and relationships. Against the Lara Croft fantasy she sets practical self-defense doctrine ('don't be there'; assertiveness, not aggression, with the bus pest), Australian, US and UN statistics on violence against women, and the Guthrie study of Chicago's feminist Thousand Waves dojo. She frames the transformation with Foucault's 'care of the self': karate's practices of the self give women power through knowledge, so that by black-belt time enduring harassment simply 'isn't who she is'.
- ch. 17 "The Way of the Place" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete) — Beattie uses Henri Lefebvre's account of the production of space to read the dojo as a 'differential space' practitioners actively create against abstract, conformist space. He shows how bow-ins, founder portraits, Japanese counting, mats, dogi and belt hierarchies mark ownership, bind the school to a lineage, separate 'dojo' from 'street', and shape bodies and safety (with Kendo's door-side seating and MMA's display of physique as hierarchy written into space). Play matters too: Aristotle's point that virtues are built by habit explains how playing at combat in a safe place breeds real courage, and the whole exercise teaches a moving balance between inside and outside.
- ch. 18 "The Perfect Weapon - Ethics and Value" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "Back at the Bins, or Loving Your Enemy Like Your Neighbor" **·** Emmanuel Levinas, Hannah Arendt, Immanuel Kant — The Face of the Other; The Categorical Imperative — Kohn begins with her own response to a serial bin-tipper: practicing iaido sword draws in full view of the neighbours to intimidate an imagined Other. Contrasting iaido's virtual opponent (a mere tool for the self) with aikido's real partners, she deploys Levinas's face of the Other, responsibility without waiting for reciprocity and philosophy as 'the Wisdom of Love', alongside Arendt's shared responsibility for the world's conflicts, to argue that care for even one's attacker comes first, with Kant's categorical imperative as the generalizable counterpart to Levinas's ethics. Her confession: she treated the imagined culprit as an object of hate, when meeting 'the Face' would have demanded an apology and maybe a hug.
- ch. 20 "Why It Matters" **·** The Buddha — Russell, who at eleven believed practice would let her kill a bull with one blow, argues that martial arts culture systematically breeds epistemic vices: gullibility (ki knockouts, chocolate milk for recovery), closed-mindedness, dojos treated like churches, sunk-cost defence of the side-kick-knifes-from-hands story, and deference to sensei and founders (Funakoshi curing fevers with karate). She diagnoses data-poverty, since lethal techniques cannot be ethically tested, as the enabling condition, and prescribes cautious belief, closing with the Buddha's counsel from Harry Cook's dojo wall: believe nothing on the authority of masters alone. It matters because these are beliefs about what can injure and kill.
- ch. 21 "The Moving Shadow of Truth" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, Aristotle, Michel Foucault, René Descartes — The Dialectic; Mind–Body Dualism; Embodiment (the lived body); Discipline and Docile Bodies — Haffner and Vogel define martial arts by a Wittgensteinian family resemblance to combat and organize the promise of self-improvement as paired opposites, working them Hegelian dialectic style, granting some truth to each side. They ask whether training brings peace or violence (Hobbes's shield for a war of all against all and Freudian catharsis versus Aristotle's worry that habituated violence breeds violence), strength fantasies or Socratic humility about weakness (with Sun Tzu's know-your-enemy and Foucault on the teacher's gaze and dojo power games), Cartesian dualism versus embodiment, and appreciation of tradition versus its distortion. The lesson is that the martial path holds both light and shadow, and separating enlightenment from self-deception takes eternal vigilance.
- ch. 22 "What Monkey Should Have Known" **·** The Buddha — Buddhism; Zen Buddhism; Karma and Rebirth — Mortensen opens with Monkey from Journey to the West beating six robbers to death despite Tripitaka's protest, and asks whether a practitioner of budo can be a Buddhist. He defends three principles, Take No Life, No First Strike and Stop Before Harm, qualifying them via the Upaya-kausalya Sutra's sea captain, Funakoshi's 'there is no first strike in karate', Ueshiba's purely defensive aikido, the initiator's bad karma, and the exception of multiple attackers; then he applies them to weapons, arguing that wooden weapons (the jo, Musashi's bokken, above all the humble walking stick, the 'last legal weapon') fit the precepts where the katana does not. Monkey, in short, should have carried a stick.
- ch. 23 "Living Beauty" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Pythagoras — The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Yin and Yang — Saltzman explains why a flowing Shaolin Kenpo form is beautiful by way of Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy: the Apollonian geometry of square, triangle and circle fuses with Dionysian power and intention, just as yang hardness needs yin softness. She grounds the body's fitness for this in the Golden Ratio known to Pythagoras, answers 'beauty is in the eye of the beholder' with Clive Bell's 'significant form' as an objective structure that trained judges can recognize, and locates 'living beauty' in the practitioner's own breakthrough, the moment when, as Nietzsche and Yeats agree, the dancer and the dance dissolve into pure mindless movement.
- ch. 24 "Excalibur - Western Martial Arts" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "Jousting for Virtue" **·** Aristotle — The Golden Mean; Virtue Ethics (arete); Practical Wisdom (phronesis) — Farrell argues that the medieval code of chivalry is a living case study for Aristotle's virtue ethics: Lancelot, 'mekest in hall and sternest to his foe', embodies the paradox C.S. Lewis names as meek and fierce 'to the nth', which Farrell reads as Aristotle's courage, the golden mean between cowardice and rashness, exercised 'to the right extent, at the right time, with the right motive'. The joust, meanwhile, was a proving ground where knightly virtues became second nature through habituated practice, since as Aristotle says 'it is no easy task to be good'. Western martial arts, he concludes, are 'moral kung fu': a fencing match with one's own standards of virtue.
- ch. 26 "Boxing, a School for Virtues" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); The Golden Mean — Marino answers colleagues who call college boxing 'teaching violence' with an Aristotelian defense: courage is the mean between fearlessness and excessive fear, and the ring is one of the few workshops where fear is actually practiced. He cites Wacquant's boxing gym as 'a school of morality' in Durkheim's sense, Rotella's 'education at the fights', and boxers like Maja Cavlovic and George Foreman on how training takes over when fear hits, to argue boxing forges emotional self-command. His challenge to his own students: 'How can you be consistently honest or just if you don't have the mettle to take a hit?'
- ch. 27 "Is Fencing a Dishonorable Art" **·** Thomas Hobbes — Ethical Egoism; The State of Nature; The Social Contract — Michaud argues that fencing is the loneliest and most egoistic martial art: alone on the strip, you seek to understand your opponent only in order to deceive them through disengages and parry-feints. He maps the bout onto Hobbes: psychological egoism, the dueling ground as a state of nature of 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short', and the referee as the Leviathan whose rules keep the bloodshed out while licensing normative egoism inside them. Testing defenses from Rand, Friedman and Carr's business 'rules of the game', he concludes that fencing kept its soldier's anything-goes ethos after the lethal stakes vanished, making it a 'dishonorable' art: a Hobbesian feast of solitude, egoism and deception.
- ch. 28 "The Personality of the Épée" *(no index entry yet)* — Lawrence asks why anyone practices the épée, an 'unmartial martial art' with no self-defense payoff, one-sided exercise value, and only stylized descent from dueling to first blood (unlike foil and saber's artificial targets and right-of-attack rules). His three answers: fencing uniquely rewards psychology, timing and dexterity over strength and pain-endurance (he prefers Odysseus's guile to Ajax's force); it continues a Bronze-Age tradition ('the history of the sword is the history of mankind'); and the named swords of epic, from Excalibur to Sting, point to the weapon's distinctive personality of courage, honor, deadliness, aesthetic fitness for purpose, and an intimacy with the opponent that Housman's saber-duel poem captures.
- ch. 29 "Back to Square One" **·** Immanuel Kant, Jeremy Bentham — Moss concedes fencing's romantic dueling aura, noting that Kant classed a killing in a duel as mere manslaughter, Bentham proposed giving duelists the protection of self-defense for the sake of honor, and Rousseau and Schopenhauer sneered at the whole business. But he argues the sport's uniqueness lies not in honor, psychology or combat origins, which it shares with other martial arts, but in a combination of rules: the blade-set distance between fencers, protective gear that makes them effectively invulnerable, right-of-way, and the return to a neutral start after each point. That combination allows the complex 'phrases' of feint and disengage that make fencing 'physical chess'; what is unique, he concludes, is a matter of rules, not romance.
- ch. 30 "And in the Blue Corner, Wearing the White Pants" *(notes)*
- ch. 31 "The University of Hard Knocks" *(notes)*
- ch. 32 "Fighting Index" *(notes)*
