## Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Popular Culture and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "AN EXTRAORDINARY GENIUS FOR MINUTIAE" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "The House that Holmes Built" **·** Baruch Spinoza, Socrates — Conatus (striving to persist); Substance Monism (Deus sive Natura) — Kate Rufa reads Holmes as Spinoza's 'just man': Watson's 'calculating machine' verdict in The Sign of the Four, his unshaken calm while baiting Moriarty before the Reichenbach leap in 'The Final Problem', and the geometric 'Book of Life' of A Study in Scarlet all show passion mastered by reason into adequate ideas and true freedom. The twist is the cocaine: shooting up between cases means Holmes sacrifices his conatus (the striving to persist in being) to keep his mind at a godlike pitch of activity, a God-complex no finite mode can sustain. Moriarty, equally rational but ruled by passive affects, is the shadow of this ideal, echoing Socrates' Apology point that harming others inevitably harms oneself.
- ch. 7 "His Work Is Its Own Reward" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Übermensch; Will to Power; The Death of God — Timothy Sexton argues the real Overman is not Doyle's flat 'calculating machine' but Jeremy Brett's Granada Holmes: the sneer with which he frees the Blue Carbuncle thief and the 'I am not retained by the police' outburst show him stepping beyond the herd's good-and-evil after the death of God. Brett's theatrical style, from the pivot before Lady Brackenstall in 'The Abbey Grange' to 'Gentlemen, we can do better than that' in 'The Norwood Builder', enacts Nietzsche's grand art of giving style to one's character, sublimating nihilistic dread into the pleasure of proving superiority. Where Rathbone-era Sherlocks solve crimes for truth, justice and the Victorian Way, Brett's Holmes makes the work its own reward, satisfying Nietzsche's demand that the Overman 'attain satisfaction with himself'.
- ch. 8 "Education never ends Watson. It is a series of lessons with the greatest for" **·** Edmund Gettier, Bertrand Russell, G.E. Moore — The Gettier Problem; Reliabilism; Possible Worlds — J. Solomon Johnson asks whether Holmes's conclusions are knowledge or luck, walking through justified true belief with a Holmesian Gettier case (Watson rightly believing the killer was a former ship hand for the wrong reason), Moore's proof that knowledge entails belief, and Russell's stopped clock as an unsafe belief. BBC Sherlock's fake Vermeer and the 2009 film's 'resurrected' Lord Blackwood illustrate beliefs that fail safety or sensitivity across nearby possible worlds, while 'The Stock-Broker's Clerk' shows Holmes's observation of the scorched slippers making his belief sensitive. The verdict: Holmes is justified by the track record of his own expert methods, a professional billiards player rather than a beginner's-luck fluke, though real-world imitators could never rule out enough alternatives to match him.
- ch. 9 "Birlstone Manor Revisited" **·** Martin Heidegger — Dasein (being-there); Being-Toward-Death — Fiona Tomkinson stages a Watson-Holmes dialogue in which Holmes, reworking The Valley of Fear's Birlstone Manor investigation, defines a thing as a thing of no consequence and an object as a thing transformed into a clue: the half-burned candle proving the witnesses lied, the single dumbbell used to sink Baldwin's clothes in the moat, the wedding ring and the hammer, each read through the human fear and care that moved them. A postscript has an aged Watson in 1926 discover Heidegger's newly published Being and Time and recognize his own friend's method in it: Dasein's care and being-toward-death, the directionality of equipment, and the ready-to-hand versus present-at-hand distinction, joking that Holmes might have sued Heidegger for theft of intellectual property.
- ch. 10 "A Toolbox for Your Holmes" **·** Charles Sanders Peirce, Socrates — Socratic Method (elenchus) — Sami Paavola and Lauri Jaervilehto reconstruct the textbook on detection Holmes never wrote: following Jaakko Hintikka's interrogative (Socratic) model, where the right question cracks the case, as with the dog that did nothing in the night-time in 'Silver Blaze', and Peirce's triad of deduction, induction and abduction, the backward reasoning from effects to causes exemplified by the Watson-just-from-Afghanistan chain in A Study in Scarlet. They add Peirce's categories of Firstness, Secondness and Thirdness to show Holmes succeeds because he fuses imagination and reverie with fieldwork, experiment and exact inference. The chapter closes with a twelve-point practical toolbox distilled from the canon.
- ch. 11 "A DOG REFLECTS THE FAMILY LIFE" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "Final Recommendations" *(no index entry yet)* — Francine Sanders, a former Chicago police-misconduct investigator, rereads the 1939-46 Rathbone films (The Secret Weapon, The Spider Woman, The Woman in Green) against the hard-boiled world of Chandler and Hammett. Holmes's tea-pouring intimacy with Watson, his disguises (book peddler, roughneck sailor, bogus postman after faking his death), his puzzle-obsession rather than femme-fatale obsession with Adrea Spedding, and the closing vigil over a London where 'women can come and go in safety' mark him as the hopeful, partnered opposite of the alienated loner of noir, whose corrupt city always wins.
- ch. 13 "The Postmodern Condition" **·** Jacques Derrida, Friedrich Nietzsche — Deconstruction; Binary Oppositions — Rafe McGregor claims The Hound of the Baskervilles is not a detective story at all: the hound that never bites anyone and Holmes's failure to foresee fog on Dartmoor are, via Derrida's Of Grammatology, the aporia and re-mark where the mystery-horror hierarchy of the text deconstructs. He then applies Noel Carroll's philosophy of horror, the phosphorus-painted hound as a category-crossing monster producing fear plus disgust and Grimpen Mire as horror geography, to reclassify the novel as gothic horror alongside Frankenstein, Jekyll and Hyde and Dracula. The final section ties the book's enduring mass appeal to the postmodern condition, tracing the collapse of certainty from Nietzsche's prophecies about the end of Christian values to Derrida's claim that truth is never finally available, leaving anxiety as the novel's real engine.
- ch. 14 "Chapter 8 - The Case of the Dangerous Detective" **·** Karl Marx, Socrates, Aristotle, René Descartes — Ideology and False Consciousness; Dharma — In a Platonic dialogue, Ronald Green and D.E. Wittkower argue the detective is dangerous because knowledge itself threatens a society's ideology: Oedipus's fatal investigation, the Athenian prosecution of Socrates and Anaxagoras, and Holmes's exposure that genteel Victorian society breeds the same crimes as the slums (while the hard-boiled PI shows official authority cannot deliver), with Aristotle's catharsis re-described as ideological enforcement that teaches audiences not to question social foundations. They then widen to Indian traditions: Vyasa dividing knowledge into the Vedas like an inverted Descartes, Krishna's two paths of inquiry in the Bhagavad Gita, and the Ramayana's dharma, where Rama's trial of Sita upholds cosmic order over truth, compared with the film Raavan, to ask whether ruling by an upheld lie is the greater danger.
- ch. 15 "An Eye for an Eye" **·** Alasdair MacIntyre — Virtues, Practices and Traditions; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Mihaela Frunza and Anatolia Bessemer use MacIntyre's Whose Justice? Which Rationality? to frame Holmes's casual felonies, the disguised-clergyman trick on Irene Adler, freeing Captain Croker after staging a mock courtroom in 'The Abbey Grange', and compounding a felony with Isadora Klein in 'The Three Gables', as one tradition of justice among several with no neutral court of appeal. Against the police's letter-of-the-law tradition stand the criminals' own codes of retribution, above all Jefferson Hope in A Study in Scarlet letting 'the high God judge' between the poisoned and harmless pills, making Holmes and his prey mirror-image vigilantes who prefer restitution or chivalric acquittal to statutory punishment.
- ch. 16 "The Game Is (and Isn’t) Afoot" *(no index entry yet)* — Tom Dowd argues you can never be Holmes: books and films offer only passive immersion, the flow Csikszentmihalyi describes and Marie-Laure Ryan's narrative-as-virtual-reality, with the plot pre-decided, while Holmes video games from The Riddle of the Crown Jewels to Sherlock Holmes vs. Jack the Ripper's Deduction Board supply agency and affordances for shooting and searching but offload actual deduction onto the player, who lacks Holmes's expert domain knowledge catalogued in Watson's 'his limits' list. Hence the genre's sleight of hand: Watson becomes the player's stand-in while Holmes confirms the conclusions, and BBC Sherlock's floating observation text reproduces the same trick on television.
- ch. 17 "But the Contradictions! What about the Contradictions" *(no index entry yet)* — Ivan Wolfe asks what makes the Holmes canon (fifty-six stories and four novels) authoritative, importing the religious vocabulary of canon and apocrypha, plus Star Trek and Star Wars practice, to test borderline texts: the two Doyle tales found only in French editions ('The Man with the Watches' and 'The Lost Special'), 'The Field Bazaar', Queen Mary's Dolls' House story 'How Watson Learned the Trick', and the Gillette play that coined 'Elementary, my dear Watson'. He proposes five canon criteria (by Doyle, published in his lifetime, about Holmes, non-contradictory, prose fiction) and closes by showing Sherlockians handle internal contradictions, Watson's migrating Jezail wound and Holmes's 'Nil' philosophy grade, exactly as believers harmonize scripture: explain, deny, or await further research.
- ch. 18 "I THINK YOU MIGHT WANT A LITTLE UNOFFICIAL HELP" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "Surviving Fusion" **·** Plato, Derek Parfit, Robert Nozick — Philosophy of Love; Personal Identity — Amy Kind asks whether the Holmes who marries Laurie R. King's Mary Russell could still be Holmes, weighing Aristophanes' speech in Plato's Symposium (Zeus split the original spherical humans, and love seeks our lost half) against Derek Parfit's fusion case from Reasons and Persons, in which two people grow into one body, which we would all find horrifying. Against Nozick's account of love as becoming a 'we', Delaney's merger and Gaylin's 'fused identity', she deploys Marilyn Friedman's federation model, lovers as sovereign states forming a flexible third entity, to argue that Holmes and Russell's marriage survives because its fusion reshapes identity without obliterating it: his 'half a creature with two brains and four eyes' and her refusal of the nickname 'Zherlock Mary' show both lovers keeping separate selves.
- ch. 20 "The Best Kind of Friend" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Virtue Ethics (arete); Moral Relativism — Ruth Tallman tests Holmes and Watson against Aristotle's requirement in the Nicomachean Ethics that perfect friendship exists only between the 'alike in excellence': since the two live by irreconcilable moral codes (Holmes's cocaine and burglaries versus Watson's clean living and law-abidingness), Aristotelian moral naturalism denies they can be true friends at all, despite the raw panic in 'The Three Garridebs' proving mutual devotion. Recasting the pair as moral pluralists with different 'good for me's, she argues Holmes is actually the better friend, an 'integrity-promoting' friend who urges Watson to stay home from the Milverton burglary to honor Watson's own code, while the proselytizing Watson, who nags about cocaine yet tags along anyway, repeatedly violates his own integrity.
- ch. 21 "Defiant Male Behavior" **·** Judith Butler — Gender Performativity — Julia Round traces Holmes from Baden-Powell's Scouting for Boys, which told scoutmasters to teach 'Sherlock-Holmesism', through Victorian essentialist masculinity, 'true, cold reason', stoicism under the poison darts of The Sign of the Four, yet violin, moods and the feminized domesticity of Baker Street, to argue Doyle's stories already unsettle gender essentialism. Gregory House of House, built from the same blueprint (221B, a shooter named Moriarty, a lost love named Adler, Wilson as Watson), embodies and mocks both the 1980s 'new man' and the 1990s 'new lad', cooking, soap operas, manipulation, Segways and the 'Rubik's complex', landing in Judith Butler's world where gendered behavior is a performance and masculinity is fallible, immature, and constructed.
- ch. 22 "The Honorable, the Woman" **·** David Hume — Problem of Induction; Objectification — Mona Rocha and James Rocha charge that Holmes's 'deduction' is really Humean induction, and that his inductive shortcuts about women, tricking Mrs. Smith in The Sign of the Four, reading Mary Sutherland's pacing as a love affair, and dismissing Lady Frances Carfax as a 'stray chicken in a world of foxes', are hasty generalizations made dangerous by gender stereotype. Watson is worse: his 'experience of women... over many nations and three continents' reads Mary Morstan's soul off her face and grants full courtesy only to the beautiful intruder of 'The Solitary Cyclist', a feminist case study in objectification. Irene Adler's escape in 'A Scandal in Bohemia', disguising herself as a young man and outwitting the fire ruse, is Doyle's deliberate proof that treating women as a class fails, making her a proto-feminist decades before Poirot's Rossakoff or Spade's O'Shaughnessy.
- ch. 23 "THERE ARE UNEXPLORED POSSIBILITIES IN YOU" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "Wrapping Up the Case" **·** Immanuel Kant, Augustine of Hippo, Friedrich Nietzsche — Deontology — Don Fallis organizes the whole canon as a casebook in the epistemology of deception: why characters deceive (concealing crimes like Dr. Roylott's speckled band, committing them like John Clay's Red-Headed League tunnel, Holmes's own smoke-rocket trick on Irene Adler and his faked death at the Reichenbach Falls), how they deceive (Bell and Whaley's hide-the-truth versus show-the-false, unpacked through disguises as masking, repackaging, dazzling, mimicking, inventing and decoying), and how deception is detected, by microexpressions avant la lettre or by inconsistency, as in 'The Problem of Thor Bridge'. Along the way he sorts lying from false implicature (Inspector Baynes's 'I didn't say so'), lies of omission and bald-faced lies, invokes Kant's absolute ban on lying and Augustine's taxonomy of lies, and asks whether Holmes's belief in Moriarty's web, where the absence of evidence counts as evidence, is rational inference or self-deception.
- ch. 25 "Is It All Meaningless" **·** John Stuart Mill, Charles Sanders Peirce, Plato, Aristotle, Socrates, Jacques Derrida, Ludwig Wittgenstein — Rory Kraft adopts the Great Game premise that Watson (not Doyle) wrote the memoirs and shows Watson is an untrustworthy narrator, the Jezail bullet migrating from shoulder to leg, the Tuesday March 4th murder that cannot fit the 1882 chronology, then borrows Socrates' complaint in the Phaedrus that writing 'stands in solemn silence' when questioned, so the texts cannot be cross-examined. He argues Holmes's real method is Mill's System of Logic (the Method of Residues behind 'eliminate the impossible') plus Peirce's abduction rather than deduction proper, and that Aristotle's Metaphysics ideal of truths amassing explains the Holmes brothers' knack. Failed attempts to date 'The Disappearance of Lady Frances Carfax' leave truth underdetermined, nudging toward Carnap's verdict that the unverifiable is 'meaningless' and Wittgenstein's Tractatus silence, while Derrida's 'truth is always that which can be repeated' at least settles one thing: the deerstalker was never worn.
- ch. 26 "That Far-Away Look" **·** Plato — Theory of Forms — Lahr argues that Holmes's crime-solving is an art rather than a forensic science: like his inspiration Oscar Wilde, Holmes is an aesthete whose 'aesthetic sight' perceives the criminal-artist's design in clues, so that Watson the philistine ('What ineffable twaddle!') consistently misses what is self-evident to Holmes. He suggests Plato would say Holmes sees only the perfect Forms behind appearances, and reads the BBC adaptations accordingly: in The Case of the Silk Stocking Holmes's trance-like perception of the victims' pedicured feet reveals a killer with a foot fetish, while Sherlock's 'A Study in Pink' renders his insight as first-person vision with on-screen data. The queer coding (the Diogenes Club, Moriarty's 'hereditary tendencies,' Holmes as Wilde's physical and temperamental double) links Holmes to the first sexologists' puzzle of how marginal men recognize one another at a glance.
- ch. 27 "An Inexact Science" *(no index entry yet)* — Demeter argues that Holmes's official self-image as a cold 'reasoning machine' is an ideology that distorts his actual practice: between collecting facts and eliminating impossible scenarios, Holmes is a creator of stories whose 'narrative imagination' invents possible explanations, a phase deduction cannot account for (Peter Lipton's point that Holmesian 'deduction' is not logically valid). Reading 'The Man with the Twisted Lip,' he shows how the same facts (coins in the coat pockets) become different evidence in different narratives until Holmes reconceives Boone and Neville St. Clair as one person. Holmes's preference for the bizarre over the simple, his warning against theorizing before the data, and his claim that his gift is hereditary ('Art in the blood is liable to take the strangest forms') all show detection is closer to art than science, though the scientific persona lends him professional legitimacy and lets him train Scotland Yard.
- ch. 28 "HOLMES IS A LITTLE SCIENTIFIC FOR MY TASTES" *(front)*
- ch. 29 "The New Man or the Old" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Karl Marx — The Death of God; The Meaning of Life; The End of Grand Narratives — Marks reads Holmes as the paragon Victorian whose faith in reason mirrors his era's confidence and, underneath it, its anxiety: Holmes's outburst in 'The Cardboard Box' ('What is the object of this circle of misery and violence and fear?... That is humanity's great problem to which Reason, so far, has no answer') appears the same year Nietzsche published 'Gott ist tot' in The Gay Science, amid Marx's 'opium of the people' and Darwin's displacement of religion. Reinterpreting the 2009 Ritchie film, he rejects the obvious religion-versus-reason reading of Lord Blackwood: Blackwood's 'magic' is really chemistry and machinery (technocracy), Holmes's science serves the military (dictatorship), and Moriarty (terrorism) defeats both, dramatizing post-9/11 fears about the militarized fruits of Reason. He concludes that Holmes straddles the Victorian and postmodern divide and that replacing religion with science is Rationalism's 'siren song.'
- ch. 30 "Time Enough to Drink the Poison" **·** Gottfried Leibniz, René Descartes, Plato — The Best of All Possible Worlds; Stoicism; The Dichotomy of Control — Domino reads 'The Veiled Lodger' as a drama about hope in a world after God: Holmes's 'Your life is not your own; keep your hands off it' revives Plato's Phaedo argument that we are the gods' possessions, but deist-or-atheist Mrs. Ronder is unmoved, so Holmes falls back on the Leibnizian alternative to the Stoic and Cartesian 'patience without hope' — the example of patient suffering as 'the most precious of all lessons,' grounded in Leibniz's hope that the world is no 'cruel jest.' Jefferson Hope's two pill boxes in A Study in Scarlet literalize the Leibnizian link between hope and divine justice by letting God choose who dies, while Trelawney Hope's gullibility makes the surname ironic. Mrs. Ronder's true hope was reunion with Leonardo, which his death destroyed; what saves her is a new hope founded on Watson's text, since only a writer ('I have made a slight change of name and place') can change the past.
- ch. 31 "This Way Lies Madness" **·** Plato, Gottfried Leibniz, Gottlob Frege, Bertrand Russell, Ludwig Wittgenstein — Franchella takes Holmes's 'I should never marry myself, lest I bias my judgement' as the opening of the emotion-versus-logic question: Andrea Nye's feminist critique warns that casting logic as a genius's superpower underwrites oppression, as with Tonga the 'black cannibal' exhibited like a human zoo attraction in The Sign of Four, while Cellucci and Matte Blanco ground logic evolutionarily and universally in all organisms and everyday reasoning. Holmes's 'reasoning backwards' is the analytic method — the hypothesis-seeking tradition running from Plato's Republic through Cellucci, which Leibniz and Robinson objected requires intuition and divination — and the Wason test shows social, emotional framing can actually improve logical performance, against Frege's ideal of stripping feeling from thought. Via Logicomix's Russell, Wittgenstein, and Godel, and diagnoses of Holmes as bipolar or Asperger's, she suggests logic can be a false harbor from emotion, and that love might have enhanced Holmes's powers rather than clouded them.
- ch. 32 "Our Best Bet" **·** David Hume, Karl Popper — Problem of Induction; Falsificationism — Terjesen argues Mycroft surpasses Sherlock because he truly grasps Hume's Problem of Induction: Sherlock's celebrated eliminations (the three key possibilities for Cadogan West in 'The Bruce-Partington Plans') and his newspaper-ad tests are inductive, Popperian conjecture-testing that can never confirm anything, while Goodman's 'grue' shows the same evidence always supports rival explanations. Watson's failed attempt in 'How Watson Learned the Trick,' the amateur reasoner's wrong solution in 'The Lost Special,' and Holmes's own 'Norbury' failure in 'The Yellow Face' prove that a correct method guarantees nothing. Mycroft, who 'would rather be considered wrong than take the trouble to prove himself right,' implicitly embraces Reichenbach's pragmatic justification — induction is simply our best bet — and therefore hunts longer for the facts that do not fit, acting only when England's fate is at stake.
- ch. 33 "MUSIC AT STRANGE HOURS OR THAT MIXTURE OF IMAGINATION AND REALITY" *(front)*
- ch. 34 "The Essence of Perception Holmes’s Intention and Objects Intended" **·** Edmund Husserl, Martin Heidegger — Intentionality; Phenomenology — Kilroy romanticizes not the drugs but the woodshed: Holmes's cocaine sessions, violin, and clattered study cultivate a Husserlian field of consciousness in which reality is the intercourse of subject and object, so a clue (the Trichinopoly cigar ash, 'Rache' as German for revenge) only appears to a detective whose knowledge, observation, and deduction are unified — Gregson and Lestrade misread the same room in A Study in Scarlet because they theorize before the evidence. Heidegger's distinction between merely present (Vorhandenheit) and usefully present (Zuhandenheit) objects explains what counts as a clue — the lipstick-stained wineglass, not the tablecloth — and Husserl's 'things seen are always more than what we really and actually see' explains the frozen-coaster chair. Watson's see-it-to-believe-it empiricism, drained by the Afghan war, is precisely why he has no 'special powers': he never furnishes his brain-attic with the furniture that lets objects speak.
- ch. 35 "The Seven Percent Conclusion" **·** Martin Heidegger, Blaise Pascal, Søren Kierkegaard, Arthur Schopenhauer, Friedrich Nietzsche — Pendulum Between Pain and Boredom — Malloy names boredom, not Moriarty, as Holmes's true nemesis, sorting his moods through Heidegger's three types: boredom by something (the mind-reading demonstration in 'The Cardboard Box' that bores Holmes but astounds Watson), boredom with everything ('The Noble Bachelor's' 'unwelcome social summonses'), and profound boredom — the 'black moods' behind the seven-per-cent solution, which Heidegger says reveals beings as a whole in remarkable indifference. Against Schopenhauer's pendulum swinging between pain and boredom, and Nietzsche's 'against boredom even gods struggle in vain,' Pascal's and Kierkegaard's verdict that boredom is the root of all evil explains Jeremy Paul's suggestion that Holmes invented Moriarty as an equal opponent to keep the game alive. Religion, Pascal's and Kierkegaard's cure, cannot save the modern Holmes, so work, amusement, and drugs merely treat symptoms of modernity itself.
- ch. 36 "The Game’s Afoot" **·** Socrates, Aristotle — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Virtue Ethics (arete) — Littmann poses Holmes's cocaine habit as philosophy's classic akrasia puzzle: Socrates denies weakness of will, treating it as mis-measured pleasure in which nearer pleasures loom larger — the King of Bohemia risking scandal for Irene Adler's company, Sir George Burnwell's gambling, Holmes's immediate relief of boredom — while Aristotle objects in the Nicomachean Ethics that reason really is clouded by passion, the way 'Black Peter' Carey's murderous violence is clouded by rum, so the cure is habituated practice rather than a science of measuring pleasures. Aristotle's account fits our sense that Holmes, 'the most perfect reasoning and observing machine,' knowingly chooses the lesser good. The verdict is that this is the one case Holmes failed to solve: it was Watson, not Holmes's own reason and will, who 'weaned him from that drug mania.'
- ch. 37 "The Awakened One" **·** The Buddha — Buddhism; Zen Buddhism; Impermanence (anicca) — Callis reads Holmes as a Buddhist practitioner despite the cocaine and the cigars in the coalscuttle: 'You see, but you do not observe' and 'The emotional qualities are antagonistic to clear reasoning' match Vipassana bare attention and the Theravada ideal of the cool, rational, emotionally distant sage, and his improvised violin scraping works like Thich Nhat Hanh's walking meditation — a witness without commentary. The picture is completed by Doyle's Buddhism of Ceylon in The Sign of Four, Holmes's two years 'spending some days with the head lama' in Tibet ('The Empty House'), and his sitting 'like some strange Buddha' in 'The Veiled Lodger.' She maps his method onto the Yoga Sutras' dharana, dhyana, and samadhi — patient attention to the blood-scratched plaster, sustained fixation on the crime scene, ego-surrendering contemplation — making Holmes an 'awakened one' who loves truth for its own sake while Watson lives on autopilot.
- ch. 38 "THE TRACING OF FOOTSTEPS" *(front)*
- ch. 39 "The Adventure of the Time-Traveling Detective" *(no index entry yet)* — Michaels argues that BBC's Sherlock is not a straight adaptation like the Jeremy Brett series but a Fredric Jamesonian pastiche — a hip-hop-style mash-up that samples 'A Study in Scarlet' (Watson's PTSD return from Afghanistan, the 'Rache' clue now reversed into the password 'Rachel'), the video game Heavy Rain (palette, focal blur, on-screen deduction text in the Johnston font), and TV-thriller codes, with 'The Great Game' cramming five bomb-ticking mysteries worthy of 24. Following Jameson's claim that new periods only re-weight elements already given, Sherlock's era simply promotes what was subordinate in Doyle — the misanthropy swells into 'a high-functioning sociopath,' telegrams become texts, the Irregulars become a homeless network — while the core faith in empirical reason stays untouched. Technology supplies data, but only Holmes's ability to see a narrative chain solves the crime; even Lestrade with the same gadgets could not.
- ch. 40 "The Evil Genius that Turns Moriarty into a Brain in a Vat" **·** René Descartes, Friedrich Nietzsche — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Brain in a Vat; The Cogito; The Simulation Hypothesis — Samardzija reads Star Trek's holodeck Moriarty as Descartes updated: Data plays Holmes on the holodeck while Dr. Pulaski's Nietzschean jibe (from 'The Illogical Necessary' in Human, All Too Human) denies that computation can be human, and the holographic Moriarty proves his sentience not by deduction but by feelingCrowded intuitions first and then invoking Descartes' cogito ergo sum to Picard. In 'Ship in a Bottle' he nests a simulation of the Enterprise inside the Holmes holodeck to trick the crew into believing he has escaped — an evil-genius, brain-in-a-vat scenario that ends with Picard admitting our own reality 'might be nothing more than an elaborate simulation.' The paradox is that only the unemotional android Data can detect the deception, so rationality bars him from humanity while Moriarty stays eternally deceived into thinking he has become human — and Doyle's own 'hereditary tendencies' account of Moriarty's evil, the chapter notes, is a Victorian biological determinism the hologram rebels against.
- ch. 41 "Dreams of Dogs and Butterflies" **·** Zhuangzi — Zhuangzi's Perspectivism (butterfly dream) — Clements opens and closes with Zhuangzi's butterfly dream to frame Sherlock Hound: are we watching humans who behave like dogs (zoomorphism) or dogs who behave like humans (anthropomorphism)? He then traces the media history that transformed Holmes in Japan — Natsume Soseki's London sojourn during The Hound of the Baskervilles bearing fruit in the cat's-eye satire I Am a Cat, the 'Meiken' (Famous Dog) retitlings of Rin Tin Tin and Lassie, the mukokuseki 'denationalized' economics of animal protagonists, and Miyazaki's talking-dog series stalled by the Doyle estate's copyright protest. Zhuangzi's question about dreams and reality, Clements concludes, 'remains unanswerable,' even as his butterfly emerges from its 'transnational chrysalis as an altogether different animal.'
- ch. 42 "Case Closed" **·** Jean Baudrillard — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Burnham stages the murder of reality itself and solves it with Baudrillard: the deerstalker, Inverness cape, and calabash Holmes of The Real Ghostbusters' 'Elementary My Dear Winston' is a simulacrum built from Paget's illustrations, stage actors' pipes, and the never-spoken 'Elementary, my dear Watson' — a copy of copies referring only to earlier simulations, never to Doyle's texts. Because the media-saturated everyman Winston (Baudrillard: whoever is underexposed to the media is desocialized) recognizes the 'belief made manifest' specters while the doctorate-holding Ghostbusters cannot, and because the hyperreal Holmes, Watson, Moriarty, and Hound are immune to proton packs, the simulacrum has 'murdered' its referent and become more real than the real. The 2008 UKTV poll — 58 percent of Britons believe Holmes was real while 47 percent call Richard the Lionheart mythical — proves the murder happened in our universe too, committed by the world's greatest detective.
- ch. 43 " . . Blurring the Boundaries" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein — Language Games — Duncan examines the Sherlockian Game — the century-old practice, founded in Ronald Knox's 1911 parody 'Studies in the Literature of Sherlock Holmes,' of treating Holmes and Watson as real people — through Wittgenstein's account of 'game' in Philosophical Investigations: no common feature defines games, only family resemblances, so the playful-seeming Game legitimately spans idle fun and serious scholarship. Huizinga's 'magic circle' supposedly walls games off from the world, but the Game has blurred that boundary from the start, as fans reconcile why Watson's wife calls him 'James,' hunt the real King of Bohemia, and see their labors honored in Ritchie's bull-pup and Sherlock's James Phillimore. The epistemological payoff is that knowledge and meaning do not reside in the text alone: Game-players playfully shape what they uncover, donning Canonical names like Duncan's own 'Silver Blaze,' so media fandom becomes a way of making knowledge.
- ch. 44 "All the Queen’s Horses" *(no index entry yet)* — Rennes answers why Holmes remains the greatest detective through Bakhtin: against the Queen's two bodies (Kantorowicz's natural body and body politic), Holmes channels the folk's grotesque collective body — the outré cases he loves, from geese with blue carbuncles to twisted-lip beggars — and turns the Strand's one-sitting stories and Watson's direct address into a new carnivalesque print marketplace where readers live the game rather than watch it. Holmes plays the fool-king: staging fires and revelatory horse-returns to jest at Lestrade and Colonel Ross, donning masks up and down the social ladder, pardoning John Turner and watching Milverton die, and deciphering the Musgrave Ritual to reassemble Charles II's crown as if it were rightfully his — before stepping off the throne and crediting Scotland Yard. That carnivalesque play, not forensic skill, is why Holmes is the prototype superhero who returns from Reichenbach and outlives the Crown.
- ch. 45 "HE IS A MAN OF HABITS AND I AM ONE OF THEM" *(front)*
- ch. 46 "The Very Smartest of Our Detective Officers - For Whose Future Holmes Had High Hopes" *(notes)*
- ch. 47 "His Ignorance Was As Remarkable as His Knowledge" *(notes)*
- ch. 48 "Hullo! Hullo! Good Old Index!" *(notes)*
- ch. 49 "Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 50 "Copyright Page" *(front)*

## Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Soccer and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Popular Culture and Philosophy® Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Dedication" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Soccer and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Warm-up" *(no index entry yet)* — Editor Ted Richards's introduction strips soccer to its one rule—move the ball into the net without using your hands—and argues that the passions this simple game ignites across every nation, class, age, and gender must spring from the same human wellspring as philosophy itself, so that studying soccer is a study of humanity. He frames the volume's perennial questions (what makes a thing that thing, what is the right thing to do, what makes something beautiful) as arising out of our being rather than academic invention, and previews the book's pairing of philosophers (Kierkegaard, Aristotle, Plato, Nietzsche, Kant, Dewey, Sartre) with players (Pelé, Maradona, Zidane, Cristiano Ronaldo, Messi, Fàbregas, Beckenbauer) across thirty-one chapters by forty authors from fifteen countries.
- ch. 8 "Acknowledgements" *(notes)*
- ch. 9 "FIRST HALF - The Nature of the Game" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "Football as Part of Real Life" *(no index entry yet)* — Hoyningen-Huene asks why anyone cheers a ball crossing an arbitrarily defined line and answers with his thesis that football re-enacts the drama of life: an unpredictable, fractal mixture of ability and chance—from a bobbling pitch to Manchester United's 1999 injury-time comeback and Maradona's unpunished Hand of God—mirroring the luck, skill, and irreversible injustice of real life. He analyzes the Laws of the Game as having four functions: guaranteeing equal conditions, generating analogies to life's drama, ending the drama at a knowable moment (unlike life's open-ended conflicts), and keeping the game safely distanced from real seriousness, which is why he reads hooligans as people who cognitively mistake the game's drama for a real-life fight. Finally he argues that money, careers, betting, and even the political channeling of Hungary's 1954 World Cup defeat into the 1956 uprising are secondary entanglements parasitic on a primary fascination already present in a nameless village-league match, which no other sport matches in variability of the ability–chance mixture.
- ch. 11 "The Good Gossip" **·** Plato — Theory of Forms; Possible Worlds — Borge weighs Jimmy Sirrel's claim that the best team always wins and the rest is gossip against Alex Ferguson insisting his side played better in a 1–4 defeat to Liverpool, framing the dispute as football Nominalism (only particular matches and results exist) versus football Platonism (an ideal way of playing exists over and above results). He rejects the Platonic ideal as metaphysically impossible—two perfect teams could never both score on every chance while conceding nothing, and style comparisons like catenaccio versus Brazil 1970 collapse without appeal to results—and instead uses possible-worlds counterfactuals: a team can be 'really' best yet unlucky when it creates objective scoring opportunities, like John Terry's slipped 2008 Champions League penalty or Spain's wrongly disallowed golden goal against South Korea in 2002, that go in across the closest possible worlds. Since Liverpool's deeply unfair 2005 comeback in Istanbul is celebrated as a classic, football is fiction and drama rather than a fairness-measuring contest, and the resulting what-if moaning is the good gossip that makes barstool debate worthwhile.
- ch. 12 "Oh to Be a Gooner" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Death of God; The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Will to Power; The Übermensch — Kilpatrick reads Nietzsche's madman's question 'what sacred games shall we have to invent?' as answered by the stadium: after the death of God, soccer has replaced religion as the shared narrative where modern communities make and worship heroes. Using The Birth of Tragedy, he reads a goal as an Apollonian–Dionysian fusion—the scorer's individuated ecstasy merging with the collective joy of teammates and fans—and, on Nietzsche's claim that existence is justified only as an aesthetic phenomenon, argues the game is defensible only when played creatively and artistically rather than by negative, win-at-all-costs tactics. Nietzsche's rejection of nationalism (the state as 'the new idol', the 'good European', Zarathustra's 'children's land') means club over country, and Wenger's Arsenal—with its dietary and training laboratory at London Colney cultivating an Overman, its Invincibles season, and its young, passport-blind signings—emerges as the club Nietzsche would support through its very will-to-power.
- ch. 13 "Extra Time" **·** Aristotle — The Four Causes; Virtue Ethics (arete); The Golden Mean — Kent argues soccer is Aristotle's favorite sport because everything in both is organized around the goal: the four causes explain shinguards (plastic, curved shape, Mitre's workers, protection) and the game itself, with the final cause—scoring—defining a thing's identity and goodness, so two differently made balls are both soccerballs if kicked toward a net. Soccer best fulfills sport's three purposes (physical and moral discipline, theatrical imitation with catharsis, recreation): its ninety minutes of uninterrupted continuity force hundreds of renewed acts of self-mastery in Aristotle's sense of courage and the right amount, its single referee with limited powers embodies Aristotle's preferred limited monarchy, and Argentina's sportsmanlike throw-in returning the ball after Cameroon kicks it out for an injured player exemplifies equity—making a rightful exception to the letter of the law. Own goals, where a defender's error harms his own side, supply the hamartia of Aristotelian tragedy, giving fans a healthy catharsis of pity and fear.
- ch. 14 "How Beckenbauer and Zidane Practiced the Four Cardinal Virtues" **·** Plato — Theory of Forms; Tripartite Soul; Justice in the Republic — Coumoundouros explains soccer greatness through three Platonic ideas: the Form of the footballer, which Pelé (1,281 goals, three World Cups, the save by Banks his header 'infected' with greatness and the infamous miss against Uruguay) and Maradona (the Hand of God and the Goal of the Century past five English defenders) approximate as near-perfect imitations, with position-specific Forms like forward Form for Pelé and attacking-midfielder Form for Maradona. Excellence as performing a proper function well (Republic 353a) then accounts for modern players—Ronaldo's evolved winger role, Henry converted by Wenger into a striker, Marta averaging a goal per game proving women's soccer equals the men's. Finally the Republic's four cardinal virtues grounded in the tripartite soul apply off and on the pitch: Beckenbauer playing the 1970 'Game of the Century' with a fractured clavicle and marshaling the 1974 final shows courage, wisdom, and moderation in just balance, while Zidane's 2006 head-butt on Materazzi shows the spirited part overwhelming reason, and with it greatness itself.
- ch. 15 "But an FC Bot-celona" **·** Alan Turing — The Turing Test — Drawing on their RoboCup experience—including the first human-versus-autonomous-robot exhibitions against Osnabrück (2007) and Stuttgart (2009), which the humans easily won—the authors ask whether robots could ever play rather than merely mimic soccer, proposing a modified Turing test: if a robot team's match is recognizable to fans as soccer, robots can play. Since the Laws of the Game tacitly assume human players, they design rules for a human–robot match that preserve soccer's essence—a game of limited, differently capable, fully autonomous players who must pass and move off the ball—banning goal-sized robot walls, wireless communication, software-coach micromanagement, and superhuman speed or size, much as tournament chess had to adapt its rules for Deep Blue versus Kasparov and as Oscar Pistorius's blades raised fairness questions in the Olympics. A robot victory under these 'stacked against the machines' rules, they conclude, could only come from better finesse, teamwork, and vision, and would settle on the pitch whether an FC Bot-celona can genuinely play the beautiful game.
- ch. 16 "Added Time" **·** Thomas Aquinas, David Hume — On Miracles; Free Will vs Determinism — McDermid takes Maradona's cheeky 'a little with the head of Maradona and a little with the hand of God' claim literally and asks what would make either 1986 goal against England—the obvious handball or the Goal of the Century—a miracle, using Aquinas's definition of miracles as intentional divine acts beyond the order commonly observed in nature. He explores how God could intervene without breaking natural law, analogizing God to a goalkeeper exempt from the handball rule or a spectator outside the game: in a deterministic world He could only arrange initial conditions (a domino setup requiring fine-tuning at the Big Bang), while in an indeterministic quantum world He could load the chancy micro-events along Maradona's mazy, sensitively balanced run. Hume's empiricist argument against miracles then shows we could never be justified in believing either goal miraculous, since the mundane explanation—Maradona's cheek and skill, lapses of concentration, a missed handball call—always has the whole of past experience on its side.
- ch. 17 "INTERMISSION - The Unwritten Rules" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "Luck as Anathema" **·** Moral Luck — Eylon and Horowitz defend the maligned manager's excuse 'we outplayed them and were plain unlucky' by distinguishing genuine football luck from fluke-luck: unlike sprinting, where outrunning your opponent and finishing fourth is incoherent, football's rules constitute rather than merely measure the skill, and 'almosts'—Roritania City hitting the woodwork eight times while United's one sloppy shot goes in—show ability and success genuinely coming apart. The accusation that football rewards the undeserving then exposes the control condition of moral desert, illustrated by two assassins whose shots differ only by an intervening swallow and by a never-bribed referee who would have taken the money, so that the luck football manifestly displays infects morality and politics generally. Football is anathema to some fans precisely because, unlike life where luck also rules, it displays luck inside an activity explicitly designed to reward merit—yet the authors conclude that 'almosts' and the all-or-nothing scoring are also the source of the game's beauty, and nobody who loves it would have luck removed.
- ch. 19 "Does Life Imitate Soccer" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Karl Marx — Master and Slave Morality; Alienation — Minister condemns 'negative soccer'—Sunderland at 28% possession and zero shots at Old Trafford, Stoke's goalless stalemate at Anfield, Bolton's two shots at the Emirates—through Nietzsche's genealogy of morality: teams that recognize superior opponents redefine the game's goal in slave-like resentment, replacing the pursuit of excellence, creativity, courage, and honor with a safety-first legalism of not losing, just as individual diving (Ronaldo's 'superman' dive, Drogba's histrionics) betrays the strong character, while Di Canio catching the ball for the injured keeper and Arshavin protesting his own penalty display honor. Marx then explains why the tactic is structural rather than a personal failing: Premier League revenue gaps, Champions League money, Abramovich's Chelsea billions, and the $55 million cost of relegation economically compel small clubs into what Minister reads as Marxian alienation—players unable to express themselves or flourish because economic forces dictate their play. He ends asking whether life imitates soccer: whether our own financial pressures likewise price excellence, honor, and self-expression out of ordinary lives.
- ch. 20 "Forwards Win Matches but Defences Win Trophies" **·** Immanuel Kant, Thomas Nagel, Thomas Hobbes — The Categorical Imperative; Utilitarianism; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Wall asks when the professional foul—the defender who 'had to bring him down'—could be a genuinely moral act, testing it against Kantian universalizability and the good will and against Bentham-and-Mill utilitarianism, and settling on psychologically altruistic motivation as what could override the foul's default wrongness. Against the psychological egoists (La Rochefoucauld, Slote, Hobbes) who would dissolve even Di Canio's caught ball into self-interest, he deploys Nagel's argument from The Possibility of Altruism and the soldier-on-the-grenade case, then derives tight conditions: a deliberate, minimally harmful foul, in a game it can decide, in a semifinal whose red card the fouler will certainly miss. Ballack's 2002 tactical foul on Lee Chun-Soo comes closest but fails (he stayed on the pitch), as do Schumacher's assault on Battiston, Fletcher's pointless foul at 4–0 up, and Abidal's accidental clip—so genuinely moral professional fouls are rare, but defenders get the most shots at being the team's saints.
- ch. 21 "SECOND HALF - The Beautiful Game" *(front)*
- ch. 22 "Why More Beautiful Means Morally Better" **·** Virtue Ethics — Durà-Vilà distinguishes narrow on-pitch morality (condemning dives, feigned fouls, and simulation, which no cultural permissiveness justifies) from a broader ethics of how one conducts a fulfilling life, and argues football should be appreciated two-dimensionally—result and aesthetic pleasure together—as shown by Barcelona and Real Madrid fans who grow angry at ugly play even in victory. His positive thesis is that playing beautifully is morally better: the aesthetic tradition of the Brazilian and Dutch schools, Michels and Cruyff's total football flowing into Guardiola's Barcelona, Wenger's Arsenal, and the Spain of Xavi and Iniesta promotes life-enhancing values of creativity, skill, and vision, while results-only football invites the tricks of technically limited players and managers. He concedes a dull team could be narrowly moral and a beautiful team could still dive, but maintains that beauty makes unethical play less sensible and more perverse, and that aesthetic football carries values worth exporting beyond the pitch.
- ch. 23 "The Loneliness of the Goalkeeper (Again)" **·** Immanuel Kant, Albert Camus, Ludwig Wittgenstein — Embodiment (the lived body); The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Winters celebrates the goalkeeper's fingertip save—Gordon Banks denying Pelé's header in 1970—as football's aesthetic summit, reading the keeper as the lonely, 'stark mad' outsider of existentialist fiction, a lineage he anchors in Camus, the goalkeeper of Algiers who said all he knew of morality he learnt from football. Kant supplies both the dove of the first Critique—needing the air's resistance, just as the tango's strict steps enable the dancer's personality—and the target of critique: against Kantian disinterested contemplation, he adopts Graham's Nietzschean, Dionysiac aesthetics of participation, so spectators proprioceptively feel the keeper twisting in mid-air, as Wittgenstein's question about the galloping horse picture suggests the movement enters our muscles and joints. Understanding a save or a back-heel means seeing it under a general type ('that' free kick, 'that' volley, from Beckham at Wembley back to Garrincha), and Bloch's ruminations in Handke's The Goalie's Anxiety at the Penalty Kick show the keeper alone at the liminal limit where concession and prevention meet.
- ch. 24 "Beyond Picasso and Ronaldo Living Artfully" **·** John Dewey, Plato, Aristotle — Pragmatism; Theory of Forms; Democracy as a Way of Life — Elcombe asks whether Cristiano Ronaldo, transferred to Real Madrid for $131 million—more than Picasso's Garçon à la Pipe fetched at its record 2004 auction—can be an artist like Picasso. Traditional metaphysics built on Plato's perfect Forms and Aristotle's necessary-and-sufficient conditions locks Art in a special museum realm that soccer, as a purposive sport whose beauty is only a byproduct, can never enter, leaving the game merely 'beautiful', not Art. Dewey's Art as Experience reorients the question from what art is to what art does: artworks are consummations of experience, moments of 'thatness'—that meal, that storm, that Ronaldo free kick—that lift us out of the mundane while remaining within the game's durable rules and history (Ronaldo's artistry grows from Zidane, Maradona, Cruyff, Pelé). On this pragmatist view Ronaldo is an artist in the act, the six-year-old testing a new turn on the pitch lives artfully too, and soccer's artistry becomes groundwork for communication, democracy, and the good life—doing more real work than a painting almost no one ever sees.
- ch. 25 "VHS, DVD, YouTube" **·** Immanuel Kant — Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Vargiu seats Kant in the Maracanã grandstand (after the Monty Python philosopher match) to test aesthetic disinterest against football: the judgment of taste is 'merely contemplative' and indifferent to the object's existence—explained through Gadamer's reading of the third Critique—so the gambler, the torcida chanting 'we won', the ultras, and the players themselves (whose attention and struggle preclude contemplation) all fail the test, and Kant stands alone except for the neutral spectator and the Panofsky-style purist. Kant's free versus accessory beauty explains why knowing the offside rule adds an intellectual liking to the aesthetic one (Denilson's inconclusive samba dribbles versus Garrincha's effective ones), and the second feature of taste, general validity—saying 'that Maradona goal is the most beautiful ever' claims everyone's agreement without objective rules—underwrites FIFA's Goal of the Century polls and connects the third Critique to public, communicative reason. Finally, the rewatched match on VHS, DVD, or YouTube, where the result is already known and no bets can be laid, is where fans most often approach genuine disinterested contemplation of the object's mere image.
- ch. 26 "Goals for All Ages and All Occasions" **·** Alasdair MacIntyre, Plato, Aristotle, Albert Camus — Virtues, Practices and Traditions — Opening with Camus's line that crushing truths perish from being acknowledged (and his Sisyphus, invoked to show the intrinsically interested player always wins), the authors force football to face its ugly side—divers, Pepe kicking Casquero on the ground, Catania's mooning free-kick screen, referee Pérez Burrull's robbery of Osasuna, the Heysel disaster, Bilardo pinning opponents and drugging Branco, FIFA's resistance to technology—analyzing it all with MacIntyre's account of social practices: football's constitutive rules and internal goods generate standards of excellence that cheating betrays for extrinsic rewards. Their positive ideal is the Greek Kalon, the noble-and-beautiful they field for Plato and Aristotle, exemplified when De Rossi confesses his handball goal against Messina or opponents return the ball after an injury stoppage—the beau geste uniting aesthetic grace and moral honor, as in the 4–4 Arsenal–Liverpool classic where 'neither side deserved to lose'. The ugly, they conclude, is exactly what lets the beautiful shine, as Eto'o floats over Scholes's tackle to assist a Messi goal.
- ch. 27 "FIRST EXTRA-TIME - Fandom" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "So Why Do I Support Aston Villa" **·** John Rawls — Communitarianism; The Veil of Ignorance; Utilitarianism; Moral Relativism — Rose—made a Villan by misreading a 1978 Panini sticker as Aston Villa's claret and blue—asks whether supporting Aston Villa is rational and argues ethics is far more like fandom than philosophers admit. Reasons for supporting Villa (local team, the 1982 European Cup, the colors) explain but never justify his allegiance, and the impartial procedures ethics prizes—the utilitarian benevolent spectator and Rawls's original position behind the veil of ignorance, with its 'sort of Kantian' consent-based alternative—turn out too demanding and too abstract: they would force him to donate his match ticket to charity, forbid the Premiership manager favoring his academy son, and reduce agency to the 'Rose-calcio scale' absurdity of switching to Real Madrid for rational reasons. His positive, communitarian claim is that we are thrown into social traditions whose inherited values—like a team—make moral agency and action possible at all, a 'different kind of rationality' that flirts with relativism yet still needs an exit strategy for cultures that discriminate against women or torture children.
- ch. 29 "The Final Whistle" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Eudaimonia (flourishing); Practical Wisdom (phronesis) — Andrew Lambert defends the rationality of being a football fan by updating Aristotle: living well in a liberal consumer democracy demands an accessible source of beauty, catharsis, belonging, public discourse, and altruism, and fandom trains exactly these sensibilities — from his childhood prayers for Everton to the 1914 Christmas Truce match and supporters' trusts that own clubs like Exeter City. The mature 'fan of football' takes an ironic view of the 'loyal fan's' tribal passions, gaining the practical wisdom that keeps rivalry (the Liverpool–Everton derby, the 1969 'Football War') from curdling into violence. Fandom thus answers critics who dismiss it as consumerist escapism or bad faith.
- ch. 30 "Don’t Worry, We’ll Be Back Next Season" *(no index entry yet)* — Vanhoutte argues the derby is not just a game but a clash of identity, territory and honor: old social and religious oppositions (Protestant Rangers v Catholic Celtic, Asian Fenerbahçe v European Galatasaray, Roma v Lazio's championship coffin parade) make derby loyalty a year-round collective identity in which fans win and lose as a 'we', the twelfth player. He traces this to group-identity formation through boundaries dividing the city into 'us' and 'them', showing how belonging produces both derby joy — hugging strangers, 'You'll Never Walk Alone' — and its dark side, from Figo's burnt Barcelona shirt to the Rangers fan murder of a Catholic man. Divisions only turn lethal when exaggerated, so fans must keep the rivalry a game.
- ch. 31 "The Limits of Change" **·** Plutarch, Thomas Hobbes — Ship of Theseus; Personal Identity — Osborne and Coombs turn the Ship of Theseus — every plank replaced, plus Hobbes's reassembled-planks variant — into the 'Aston Villa Paradox': with owner, manager, players, crest and even the shade of claret and blue changed, what makes it the same club fans sing 'Villa till I Die' for? Finding that presentism and Sider's four-dimensionalism cannot say which side on the 2006 pitch was really AVFC, they adopt Lynne Rudder Baker's constitution view: fans create the football-favorable circumstances that constitute a club, so it persists through total replacement of parts as long as supporters keep conferring identity and value — which is why Gareth Barry's value collapsed when he left, and why fans judged Glazer's Manchester United to have stopped existing while welcoming Lerner's Villa.
- ch. 32 "SECOND EXTRA-TIME - Soccer and Society" *(front)*
- ch. 33 "I Play Therefore I Am" *(no index entry yet)* — Foster argues football is inescapably mythic: styles of play embody national self-images, from Victorian England's muscular distrust of artistry to Argentina's criolla viveza and the compadrito, to Sebes's 'socialist' Aranycsapat, while clubs become vessels of nationalism like Athletic Bilbao's Basque-only cantera policy and Barça's 'més que un club'. Myth flows both ways — West Germany's 1954 'Miracle of Berne' restarted German patriotism, and FC Start's 1942 'Death Match' grew into a Soviet martyr myth despite its embellishments — so that, as the chapter concludes with Galeano and McNeill, what people believe matters more to a constructed social reality than what is actually true. Tell me how you play and I'll tell you who you are.
- ch. 34 "The Moment of Truth" *(no index entry yet)* — Nguyen asks what makes a team great and answers 'passion', analyzed through the philosophy of mind: passion is a dispositional state — like Stoichkov's love of the game, ascribable even while he sleeps — that manifests occurrently and causally raises the probability of success on a probabilistic theory of causation, though it is neither necessary nor sufficient for winning. The case study is Barcelona's 2008–09 treble: after the meltdown and 'madriditis' before the Bernabéu, Guardiola's passion and code of conduct restored unity, producing the 6–2 clásico, Iniesta's stoppage-time equalizer at Chelsea, and the 2–0 Champions League final win over Manchester United. Passion is what separates the great from the good.
- ch. 35 "A Little bit of Messi for our Life" **·** John Stuart Mill, John Searle, Ludwig Wittgenstein — On Liberty; The Harm Principle — The authors cast the contrast between disciplined European and improvisational South American football as Mill's struggle between liberty and authority: the coach's tactical orders are 'rules of opinion' the genius may defy, as Maradona did on his sixty-meter run to the Goal of the Century, while the harm principle marks the line at the 'rules of law' — FIFA's Laws of the Game. The Hand of God goal, which broke even a rule of law yet stood because 'a goal is scored when the referee says so', illustrates Searle's point that football's regulative capacity cannot guarantee its agreements, leaving a gap filled only by ethics and fair play. Following Wittgenstein's 'ethics and aesthetics are one and the same', they conclude that a bit of Messi-style rule-breaking — Messi replicated both Maradona goals in 2007 — is what makes football, and life, joyful and beautiful.
- ch. 36 "History and Philosophy" **·** Hannah Arendt — History Has a Direction; The End of Grand Narratives; The Public Sphere — Imre reads Hungary's Aranycsapat as a political-philosophical event: Sebes's socialist 4–2–4 football was meant to prove that cooperative civil society could flourish under Stalinism, and the 6–3 demolition of England at Wembley, with its self-organizing positional play, became the sporting antithesis to Rákosi's regime — culminating in the 1956 Revolution that Arendt cited as a 'true' revolution of spontaneous councils. The 1954 final loss to West Germany (contrasted with Germany's own rebirth at Berne) entrenched a fatalism that history's organic 'grand narrative' and 'final synthesis' were against Hungary, helping destroy the civil-society possibility the team embodied and pushing Hungarians into anti-politics. His lesson: talent and beauty can be quashed by the contingency of history — igazság, truth-justice, never manifested, and soccer could not overcome history.
- ch. 37 "A Season Ahead" **·** Niccolò Machiavelli — Borghini and Baldini analyze how a soccer club becomes a metaphorical mirror constructing its patron's public persona: the sport's unpredictability, its win/lose dialectic, and the referee's undisputed authority make it adaptable as a metaphor for life, and value-laden properties flow from club to owner through a three-step mirroring process from bare individual to owner to persona. They contrast the slowly built stile Juve of the Agnelli family with Silvio Berlusconi, who exploits mass media to link himself only to AC Milan's wins — blaming coaches or his own absence for defeats, like Machiavelli's prince overcoming fortuna — and with Maurizio Zamparini, Palermo's self-styled moral 'Leonidas' demanding democratic rules and safer stadiums. Persona construction emerges as deliberate meaning transfer, not mere image-making.
- ch. 38 "KICKS FROM THE MARK - It’s Down to Penalties" *(front)*
- ch. 39 "Choosing the Scapegoat" **·** John Stuart Mill — Free Will vs Determinism — Northcott dissects England's penalty shoot-out misery to ask whether 'bad luck' is objective or a scapegoat: what counts as luck depends on the reasonable standard of preparation, so what was bad luck twenty years ago (no practice) is negligence today, and under Laplace's demon's determinism no sixty-percent chances would exist at all. He rehabilitates objective luck relative to shared standards of reasonableness, concluding that shoot-outs genuinely are more of a lottery than open play — though not a total one. On blame, he uses the deviation-from-default account of causation and Mill's problem of causal selection to argue that singling out a referee over missed open goals or injuries has no objective justification; moral feelings and prejudice pick our scapegoats.
- ch. 40 "Double Dutch" **·** Søren Kierkegaard — Anxiety (the dizziness of freedom); Existentialism — Krnac explains Holland's five missed penalties against Italy at Euro 2000 — Frank de Boer twice, Kluivert, Stam, Bosvelt — through Kierkegaard's The Concept of Anxiety rather than Cruyff's 'chance' or Vergouw's 'poor preparation'. The self, a synthesis of body, mind and spirit (and of the temporal and eternal), must stake itself on a future-oriented choice, but freedom as 'the possibility to be able' makes every free choice an embrace of the unknown, breeding the anxiety that is 'the dizziness of freedom' — visible in de Boer's slide from a five-out-of-ten miss to a lifeless zero that telegraphed his shot to Toldo. Panenka's 1976 chip shows free action chosen without guarantee, while choosing not to choose is itself an evasion of freedom, in penalties as in life.
- ch. 41 "Splitting Hairs" *(no index entry yet)* — Saunders rebuts the complaint that penalty shoot-outs are 'lotteries': unlike the coin toss that decided Liverpool–Cologne in 1965, penalties test skill and nerve, and lotteries are not inherently unfair anyway, since giving two equally deserving kidney patients an equal chance is the fairest resort once relevant grounds run out. Fairness does not demand equal chances of winning — it demands due weight to relevant differences — so the better team should be likelier to win, yet winners are not always the better team, as Liverpool's 2005 Istanbul triumph alongside a fifth-place league finish shows. The point of a match is to decide who wins, not who is better, so penalties are legitimate precisely as a skill-testing, exciting way to separate equally deserving teams.
- ch. 42 "Refereeing in the World" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — Bad Faith; Radical Freedom and Responsibility; Authenticity — Crowe uses Sartre to explain why refereeing is existentially anguished: in the moment of decision — Grosso's fall over Neill's outstretched legs at the 2006 World Cup — the referee is radically free and solely responsible, and that anguish drives the six familiar referee types into bad faith. The stickler hides behind the letter of Law 12 as Sartre's student hid behind ethical formulas, the ditherer repeats the woman who leaves her hand inert on her date's, the poseur and frustrated player over-act the café waiter's role, and the postman and tough guy play the 'champion of sincerity' who treats character as fixed. The ideal is the authentic referee 'refereeing in the world' — Collina disallowing his own awarded goal at San Siro and explaining why to Inter — who owns his contingency: 'This is what I have chosen.'
- ch. 43 "Football and Religion Don’t Mix" *(no index entry yet)* — Majeed, writing from Ghana's 2008 Africa Cup of Nations and the Fowl Man affair, argues that 'God is not a referee': a God whose nature is rational, just and good cannot coherently be petitioned to fix match outcomes, so fans who blamed the Fowl Man's bird-charm for the semi-final loss to Cameroon — like players who point skyward à la Kaká — misunderstand both divinity and football. He offers instead an empirical account of winning (strategy, fitness, discipline, fair officiating) topped by irreducible chance, whose illogic even breaks the hypothetical syllogism, since on a lucky day Sheffield United can beat Manchester United. Chance is what keeps football a game at all, and its deeper beauty lies in expressing a common humanity — 'humanity has no boundary' — not in divine intervention.
- ch. 44 "A Phenomenology of Reading the Ref" **·** Edmund Husserl, John Dewey, Thomas Hobbes, John Rawls — Phenomenology; The Social Contract; The Veil of Ignorance — Vannatta asks what the rules of soccer are from a player's perspective and tests legal theories: natural law and Rawls's veil of ignorance are too abstract to help on the pitch, and Austin's and Hart's positivism overemphasizes FIFA's top-down commands, so the best account is legal pragmatism — Holmes's bad man treats the law as a prophecy of what the ref will actually call, and Dewey roots the rules in custom and in the whistle itself rather than in prior legislation. Husserl's genetic phenomenology then explains how 'reading the ref' is possible: retention and protention synthesized in passive synthesis let experienced players anticipate play — and the referee's tendencies — without deliberation, replacing the impoverished notion of muscle memory. Playing to the whistle becomes a trainable skill of predicting an indeterminate despot, with lessons for coaching and sportsmanship alike.
- ch. 45 "A Funny Old Game" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein — Language Games — Grimwood and Miller ask what makes a footballing cliché ('the boy done good', 'a game of two halves', 'they gave 110 percent') hearably meaningful rather than lazy, using Gadamer's hermeneutics and the later Wittgenstein. Gadamer explains clichés as part of the 'horizon' of prejudices that makes understanding the game possible at all — Ian Holloway's taxi-and-young-lady metaphor baffled because it fell outside that horizon — but Wittgenstein goes further: meaning is what words and gestures do in the language-game, so badge-kissing, like the rain dances Wittgenstein defended against Frazer's reductionism, is an expressive form of life whose sincerity or cynicism settles only in context. Even calling something a cliché is itself a move in the game.
- ch. 46 "The First Team" *(notes)*
- ch. 47 "Index" *(notes)*
- ch. 48 "Soccer and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 49 "Copyright Page" *(front)*

## South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
